@@138599071 <p> A new study from the University of Notre Dame , published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , finds that rising temperatures driven by greenhouse gas emissions are directly linked to increases in stunting , alongside persistent socioeconomic inequality . <p> Analysing data from 34 African countries over 16 years , researchers found that every 1 ? C rise in human-caused temperature anomalies corresponded to a 3.45% increase in childhood stunting . <p> The researchers say the findings show how climate change is already affecting child health through disruptions to food systems , agriculture and household incomes . <p> " A single degree of warming might sound negligible in a daily weather report , but on a global scale , it alters the foundational conditions of child survival , " said Professor ArunAgrawal , co-author of the study . <p> He said rising temperatures can reduce crop yields and increase food prices , leaving young children particularly vulnerable to malnutrition during critical stages of development . <p> " Global emissions are being directly translated into child undernutrition , " he added . <p> To isolate the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with climate models that separated natural variability from anthropogenic change . They found no meaningful link between general weather fluctuations and stunting , but a clear and statistically significant association with human-caused warming . <p> The study also highlights the role of inequality as a parallel driver of poor child health . Communities with weaker access to services such as healthcare , sanitation , clean water and maternal education were consistently more affected . <p> However , researchers say climate change does not simply amplify inequality -- it compounds it . Wealthier households are often able to buffer shocks such as droughts or poor harvests , while poorer families face deeper food insecurity and reduced access to essential services . <p> " Climate change acts as a threat multiplier on top of existing social fractures , " said Agrawal . " When a heatwave or drought hits , the poorest children are pushed furthest out of reach of basic nutrition and care . " <p> The effects were most severe in rural areas and regions with limited infrastructure . Researchers say these communities , which have contributed least to global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ insecurity . <p> Lead author NabinPradhan said the findings highlight the need for integrated policy responses that address both climate adaptation and structural inequality . <p> " Investments in education , sanitation and household resilience are not just social policies -- they are climate interventions , " he said . <p> The study suggests that improving maternal education and access to clean water and sanitation could significantly reduce stunting by improving nutrition , healthcare access and disease prevention in early childhood . <p> Researchers argue that addressing climate-driven under-nutrition requires more than environmental measures alone , calling instead for coordinated action across health , education and development policy . <p> They plan further research using long-term household-level data to better understand how climate stress and inequality interact to shape child health outcomes . 
@@138609149 <h> What happens when cities grow faster than infrastructure <p> As the rains intensify across Nigeria , familiar scenes are returning : flooded streets , submerged homes , gridlocked roads and communities cut off by rising waters . For many Nigerians , these disruptions have become an almost expected feature of the rainy season . <p> Yet they are more than seasonal inconveniences . They reveal a deeper and more consequential problem : the widening gap between the pace at which our cities are growing and the infrastructure needed to support them . <p> Heavy rainfall may trigger flooding , but it is rapid urbanisation without adequate planning that turns natural weather events into economic and humanitarian crises . Nigeria is urbanising at one of the fastest rates in the world . According to the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs , about 56 per cent of Nigerians now live in urban areas , a figure projected to approach 70 per cent by 2050 . Few countries are urbanising as rapidly as Nigeria . The question is no longer whether Nigeria will become predominantly urban ; it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> That means tens of millions more people will depend on roads , drainage systems , housing , public transport , water supply , and other urban services that many cities are already struggling to provide . This trend is not unique to Nigeria . <p> Across the developing world , cities continue to expand as people migrate in search of jobs , education , and better opportunities . Urbanisation , in itself , is not a problem . In fact , history shows that it is one of the strongest drivers of economic transformation . The World Bank describes cities as engines of productivity , innovation and employment , accounting for the overwhelming share of economic activity in most countries . Economists call these the benefits of agglomeration , the gains that arise when people and firms operate close to one another . <p> Well-planned cities create opportunities , attract investment , and improve living standards . Poorly planned ones magnify inequality , congestion , and environmental risks . Unfortunately , many Nigerian cities have expanded far faster than the infrastructure designed to support them . Drainage networks built @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ intended . <p> Roads carry traffic volumes they were never designed to accommodate . Housing development often outpaces physical planning , pushing families into flood-prone areas , wetlands , and natural waterways . Public transport remains inadequate , while waste management systems struggle to keep pace with growing populations . The consequences become painfully visible each rainy season . Floodwaters overwhelm blocked drainage channels , businesses suspend operations , commuters lose productive hours in traffic , goods are damaged , and families suffer losses that may take months to recover from . What appears to be a weather problem is , in reality , an infrastructure deficit . <p> Climate change is making these vulnerabilities even more severe . More frequent and intense rainfall means cities can no longer rely on infrastructure standards developed for yesterday 's climate . Urban resilience now requires investments that anticipate future weather patterns rather than simply responding to past disasters . This is why urban planning should no longer be treated as a routine administrative function . It is an economic imperative . <p> Infrastructure alone can not solve problems if governance remains weak @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we think about urbanisation itself . Too often , city growth is viewed as something to be managed after the fact . By then , informal settlements or slums have expanded , roads are overwhelmed , and expensive emergency interventions become the only option . A better approach is to plan , ensuring that infrastructure grows alongside population rather than years behind it . This matters because Nigeria 's urban transition is only beginning . Over the next two decades , millions more people will move into cities regardless of government policy . Theories abound that explain this attraction of urban centres . The real question is whether those cities will become centres of innovation , productivity and opportunity or increasingly congested spaces vulnerable to flooding , environmental degradation and declining quality of life . The answer depends largely on decisions being made today . <p> Investments in drainage systems , mass transit , affordable housing , digital mapping , climate-resilient infrastructure and stronger municipal governance may not always generate immediate political dividends , but they produce long-term economic returns that benefit generations . As another rainy season unfolds , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ disruptions . They are warning signs of a structural imbalance that will become more costly if left unaddressed . <p> Rain exposes weaknesses ; rapid urbanisation without matching infrastructure creates them . Nigeria can not stop its cities from growing , nor should it try . Urbanisation remains one of the country 's greatest opportunities for economic transformation . But if infrastructure continues to lag population growth , our cities risk becoming less productive , less resilient and less liveable . The real challenge , therefore , is not whether Nigeria will urbanise . It is whether we can build cities that are prepared for the future before the future arrives . <h> UPDATE NEWS : <p> Nigerians can now invest ? 2.5 million on premium domains and profit about ? 17- ? 25 million . @@138630135 <h> Education without skills is just a source of information <p> EDUCATION without skills is just a source of information . It may impress the eye , decorate a wall with certificates , or help a person recite definitions , but it does not necessarily change life , industry , community , or society . In a world where knowledge is now available at the touch of a phone screen , the real question is no longer whether people have access to information . The real question is whether education is helping them use information to solve problems , create value , build character , and improve human conditions . As a Nigerian-born Finnish scholar who has spent more than a decade in education across four national contexts and three continents , I have seen the beauty and the weakness of modern learning . I have met brilliant students who could explain theories with confidence but struggled to apply those theories to workplace realities . I have also met adults with limited formal qualifications who , through experience and practical exposure , demonstrated exceptional judgement , leadership , and resilience @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ only when it produces usable competence . <p> Education should not be reduced to the gathering of facts . Facts are important , but they are only raw materials . The value of education appears when facts are transformed into skills : the skill to think critically , communicate clearly , lead ethically , use technology wisely , understand people , manage resources , and respond to changing circumstances . A person may know the definition of entrepreneurship and still be unable to identify a market opportunity . A graduate may know theories of leadership and still be unable to inspire a team . A manager may understand digital transformation and still be afraid to use digital tools . This is the gap between information and capability . This gap is particularly visible in entrepreneurship . These spaces may seem ordinary , but they perform important functions that affect our health , economy , and environment . Parks improve physical and mental health . Climate change is no longer a distant problem . Nigerian cities are already experiencing higher temperatures and more frequent flooding . Many urban areas have become " heat islands , " meaning they are much hotter than surrounding rural areas because of too many buildings and too little vegetation . Trees and green spaces help cool the environment . They provide shade and release moisture into the air , reducing temperatures naturally . Trees also absorb carbon dioxide , one of the major gases responsible for global warming . As Nigerian cities continue to grow , planting more trees and preserving open green areas can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more comfortable . Parks , wetlands , and vegetated areas therefore reduce the risk of flooding . Unfortunately , many natural green areas in Nigeria have been converted into residential and commercial developments . As a result , cities have lost important natural systems that once helped manage stormwater . Protecting and creating urban green spaces should therefore be part of every city 's flood management strategy . <p> Green spaces build stronger communities . Properties located near parks often increase in value . Beautiful and well-maintained parks attract investors , businesses , and tourists . Recreational facilities create jobs for gardeners , landscapers , security personnel , and maintenance workers . Cities around the world have discovered that investment in parks and green infrastructure yields long-term economic benefits . Nigerian cities can also benefit from such investments . <p> Children need places to play . Children are among the biggest beneficiaries of urban parks . When children lack recreational spaces , they often play on roads , in drainage channels , or in unsafe areas . This increases their exposure to accidents and other dangers . A city that does not provide spaces for its children is not planning adequately for its future . Nigerian cities are losing their green spaces . Rapid urbanisation is putting enormous pressure on open spaces across the country . Population growth and increasing demand for land have led to the conversion of many parks , gardens , and undeveloped lands into buildings . In some cases , spaces originally designated as parks in city master plans have been taken over by other developments . In others , parks have simply been neglected and allowed to deteriorate . They improve physical and mental health , reduce flooding , support economic growth , and strengthen communities . As Nigerian cities continue to expand , we must avoid the mistake of building cities of concrete alone . Nigeria possesses sufficient natural gas resources to make clean cooking energy affordable . @@138686940 <h> SCO at 25 : Expanding beyond security into sustainable development <p> 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization ( SCO ) . As one of the world 's largest regional bodies , the SCO spans countries across much of Eurasia , representing nearly half of the global population and contributing about 25% of global GDP . <p> Since its founding in 2001 , the organisation has steadily expanded its focus beyond security , actively promoting sustainable development and improving lives across the region . <p> From modernising irrigation systems on arid farmlands and equipping students with practical skills through the Luban Workshops , to expanding freight and passenger connections , the SCO has achieved tangible results in advancing sustainable development . <p> Achievements in poverty reduction , vocational education , and regional connectivity demonstrate how member states are turning cooperation into concrete benefits for their communities , strengthening both shared prosperity and regional integration . <h> Stay Ahead with Premium Times <p> Poverty reduction remains a collective priority among SCO member states . As countries across the region seek to improve living standards and promote inclusive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increasingly important area of cooperation . <p> China became the first developing country to meet the United Nations ' poverty reduction target , achieving it ten years ahead of schedule . <p> SCO Secretary-General Vladimir Norov has attributed this achievement to a combination of sustained economic growth , targeted poverty alleviation policies , investment in education , technological innovation , and environmental protection . He has also noted that China 's experience offers valuable lessons for other SCO countries pursuing their own development goals . <p> Across much of the SCO region , millions of people depend on farming and related industries for their livelihoods , making agricultural modernisation essential to improving rural incomes and promoting sustainable development . <p> According to Sheradil Baktygulov , Director of the Global Policy Institute of Kyrgyzstan , outdated irrigation and land reclamation technologies remain common challenges for many Central Asian countries , limiting agricultural productivity and rural development . <p> To address these challenges , China has been sharing modern agricultural technologies and practices with the SCO member states . Water-saving irrigation has become a major area of cooperation . <p> In Uzbekistan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's water consumption , improving irrigation efficiency is particularly important . Despite its arid climate , water-saving irrigation systems historically covered only a small share of the country 's farmland . <p> Through cooperation with China , Uzbekistan introduced drip irrigation technology on 2,000 hectares of farmland in 2024 . The project increased water-use efficiency by more than 40% while boosting cotton yields by around 30% . <p> Similar progress can be seen in Kyrgyzstan . A Chinese-supported irrigation project completed in 2021 is reportedly to provide water access for 11,100 hectares of farmland in the Batken and Issyk-Kul regions , helping around 20,000 farmers increase agricultural production and strengthen their livelihoods . <p> Beyond irrigation , seed breeding has become another important area of agricultural cooperation . <p> Wheat is a staple crop in many SCO member states . Yet climate change , water scarcity , and disease pressures continue to affect production . In Pakistan , for example , rust disease remains one of the most destructive threats to wheat crops . <p> Since 2023 , Chinese and Pakistani researchers have been working together to develop new wheat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ local Pakistani varieties . The new wheat strain has demonstrated strong adaptability to northern Pakistan and increased yields by around 9% . <p> Cooperation in seed breeding is also delivering results in Kazakhstan , a major wheat-producing and exporting country . According to the Observatory of Economic Complexity , Kazakhstan exported $1.13 billion worth of wheat in 2024 , making it the world 's 13th largest wheat exporter . <p> To further enhance production , Chinese agricultural experts worked with local farmers to introduce a new wheat variety in North Kazakhstan , one of the country 's main spring-wheat-producing regions . Since its introduction , wheat yields in the area have increased by approximately 28% . <p> This approach is now being adapted in Uzbekistan . @@138687213 <p> In its many centuries of historical evolution -- from the ancient Egyptian and Roman periods through the French and Prussian ramifications to the British iteration of its essence -- we can say , without any exaggeration , that the public service has never faced the kind of challenging reality it is confronting in the twenty-first century . While it is true that the public service has weathered every conceivable challenge , from wars to famines , droughts and economic recessions of all kinds , it now confronts all these challenges across the world in even more severe and complex forms . <p> Today , the world is in a polycrisis . This simply means not only that the world is confronted with unimaginable conflicts , problems and all sorts of predicaments , or that these crises and challenges are manifesting on a scale never before seen in any century . A polycrisis also implies that these conflicts , crises and challenges are interconnected in highly complicated ways that pose serious headaches for governments , public administrators and public managers . The challenge posed by climate change , for example @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but also about how it aggravates agriculture , ethnic conflicts , and geopolitical and geoeconomic crises across the world . Cybersecurity challenges fuel terrorism that cripples national governments and plunges nations into governance crises . And that is how every other conflict and crisis compounds and intensifies others . <p> At the heart of all these problems , challenges , crises and predicaments lies the public service , upon which every government depends to confront and address these issues through policies designed to serve citizens . On September 11 , 2001 , the United States experienced one of the largest terrorist attacks in modern history . According to one commentator , a government system that " had defeated the Nazis , the Japanese and the Soviet Union was no match for a handful of terrorists . " When the World Trade Center came tumbling down in a shower of bricks , steel and human remains , it was the American public service that shouldered the burden of responding to a catastrophe of an unimaginable scale . When the coronavirus pandemic swept across the globe from 2019 to 2021 , public @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ traumatic impact -- hospital workers , doctors , nurses , members of the armed forces , law enforcement officers , and many others . Public servants withstood the pandemic at its cruelest moments , often without the required equipment . The situation was even worse for many countries , including those regarded as the epitome of infrastructural development , whose sophisticated healthcare systems failed woefully to contain the ravaging virus . No government , policymaker or public service was fully prepared for the pandemic or for the succession of crises that have emerged , from the Internet bubble collapse of 2000 to the US-Iran conflict of 2026 . <p> This provides a useful starting point for reflecting on the state of the public service in what has been described as a VUCA environment -- a twenty-first-century environment that is volatile , uncertain , complex and ambiguous . A world in polycrisis is therefore one that generates uncertainty , ambiguity and vulnerability despite our most cherished infrastructural advancements . The VUCA environment simply implies that the public service may not always be prepared for the worst that human ingenuity and actions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concerns how governments and their public services are challenged not only to rethink their policy understanding of human progress and flourishing , but also to reconsider the very idea and structure of the public service responsible for implementing those policies . <p> Given these challenging realities within which the public service must operate , what questions confront political and bureaucratic leadership across the world ? The questions are simple but significant . First , given that many governments and public services were caught unprepared and struggled with the administrative implications of the multiple crises that have beset the world in the twenty-first century , how many more crises and upheavals are lurking within the complexities of global geopolitics and public governance that public services may be called upon to manage in the years ahead ? Second , given that the administrative lessons , skills and experiences of the twentieth century have become increasingly inadequate for addressing today 's challenges , how should governments and their public services begin the process of rethinking and reinventing government business to make it fit for contemporary administration and governance ? In other words , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ traditional Weberian public service to make it sufficiently resilient , pre-emptive and agile to enable public managers confront the VUCA environment and prepare for the decades ahead ? In what ways , for example , can the Nigerian public service become more effective and efficient in managing today 's polycrisis while preparing for future crises and learning from them ? <p> Many countries today , especially members of the Commonwealth of Nations , including Nigeria , inherited the Weberian bureaucracy . This is the largely hierarchical , rule-based and rational institution that determines the structural character of the public service . This legal-rational system promotes maximum efficiency through strict adherence to rules and procedures , respect for hierarchy and specialization . Consequently , the bureaucracy has become a stable , impersonal and highly formal institution designed to perform tasks predictably . The Weberian model of government business is therefore structured as a stabilising rather than an innovative operating system . Unfortunately , this stifles the administrative creativity and rapid adaptation required to confront disruptive challenges and innovation within the VUCA environment . <p> When the coronavirus pandemic struck , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of its rigid characteristics by adopting digital tools that enabled data-driven decision-making , greater administrative speed and improved efficiency , particularly in implementing policies relating to school closures , social distancing and other significant interventions . This facilitated more efficient resource allocation and monitoring while supporting data-driven strategic communication that enhanced public trust and compliance . However , on the downside , the system could not entirely overcome its entrenched institutional inertia and poor coordination across the three tiers of government . This was compounded by years of underinvestment and inadequate infrastructural development , particularly within the healthcare sector . The result was shortages of critical supplies , limited technological deployment and inefficient distribution of resources across the country . <p> What has been the dominant framework of change management that has shaped administrative reforms and praxis within the Nigerian public service over the years ? In other words , how has the system pursued reform , restructuring and re-engineering since independence ? I will highlight two major change management frameworks . <p> The first is the excessive reliance on global best practices , imported administrative models , external experts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ often driven by development agencies promoting neoliberal paradigms and models developed within entirely different socio-political contexts . Unfortunately , they frequently create a conception-reality gap in which reforms become largely technicist because they transplant models from one context into another that is significantly more complex . Consequently , such reforms become radically decontextualised , thereby limiting or even undermining their effectiveness . This is what happened with several reform initiatives , ranging from some public-private partnership projects to the 6-3-3-4 educational model . External experts and consulting firms also often operate without deep institutional knowledge or meaningful collaboration with insiders . As a result , they fail to generate the practical insights needed to understand institutional realities and craft appropriate solutions . On the other hand , many Ministries , Departments and Agencies ( MDAs ) often lack the necessary skills and competencies to effectively adapt these universal models to the Nigerian administrative environment . <p> The second framework has been the strengthening of institutional reform implementation through sustained investment in training and capacity building for reform managers . These efforts seek to stimulate institutional reforms and innovation by encouraging @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ within the workplace . This competency-based approach was reflected , for example , in the establishment of the Organisation and Methods ( O&amp;M ) Unit , which later evolved into the Management Services Office and was replicated across MDAs through units such as the Organisation , Operations Management and Research Unit within the Departments of Planning , Research and Statistics , and what is now known as the Reform Coordination Department . Unfortunately , these reform efforts have remained largely episodic because they have not been systematic , intentional or embedded within a comprehensive reform blueprint . Rather , they have often been triggered by accidental circumstances such as economic crises or public criticism . <h> Related News <p> All these raise a critical question for us going forward : How can the Nigerian public service fully leverage existing structures , systems and reform strategies to stimulate and deepen the generation of innovative reform solutions capable of addressing both long-standing and emerging challenges ? For me , the answer lies in context-sensitive governance reforms that seek to reconfigure public governance through innovation-driven reform strategies , especially by adopting more participatory @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , private stakeholders and society at large . Such a reform strategy requires the creation of national innovation systems that facilitate collaboration between public and private actors through reform networks and knowledge exchange , including the infusion of entrepreneurial insights . This collaborative approach harnesses local knowledge and private-sector expertise to generate what may be described as " collective intelligence , " which is likely to be more reliable and resourceful than an excessive dependence on pre-packaged imported models and paradigms . This can be strengthened by a proactive research and development ( R&amp;D ) framework that incorporates methodologies such as ethnography , participant observation and design-based approaches like prototyping . <p> If this analysis of the reform process is valid , then we can significantly broaden the scope of civil service reforms by embracing public governance domains that encourage innovative approaches capable of promoting greater social inclusion within administrative praxis . I will conclude by highlighting five such domains . <p> First , there should be a broader commitment to transparent and open government through enhanced digitalisation and automated service delivery that makes the public service more citizen-friendly while @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in policymaking should be strengthened to foster greater trust in government and its policy actions . <p> Third , to achieve a truly citizen-centred public service , the skills and competencies of public servants must also be significantly enhanced . This requires a paradigmatic shift involving new mindsets , concepts , institutional culture and attitudes . <p> Finally , there is an urgent need to build strong , multi-layered collaborations capable of driving socially inclusive reforms -- collaborations within institutions , between national and subnational governments , between the public service and innovation ecosystems , between government and society , and through a deepening of public-private partnerships . <p> Being a presentation as Guest Speaker at the Nigeria Public Service Lecture marking the United Nations Public Service Day , organised by the Bureau of Public Service Reforms ( BPSR ) on 23 June 2026 , held at Nicon Luxury Hotel , Abuja.

@@138708552 <p> For decades , Nigeria has pledged to end routine gas flaring and cut methane emissions . From children battling chronic respiratory illnesses and persistent skin diseases to mothers mourning infants lost after breathing complications , DARE AKOGUN investigates the human cost of this environmental pollution and why vulnerable communities remain exposed despite years of climate commitments <p> As dusk settles over Okwuzi , an oil-producing community in Ogba/Egbema/Ndoni Local Government Area of Rivers State , the horizon bursts into shades of orange and crimson . Even during periods usually associated with cooler weather , residents complain of intense heat that hangs over their communities like a heavy blanket . <p> They say the heat is more than uncomfortable ; it is suffocating . Increasingly , they fear it is making them sick . <p> When Sunday PUNCH visited the communities , it found a troubling pattern of health complaints that residents believe is linked to decades of exposure to emissions from nearby oil and gas facilities . <p> Infant deaths <p> For 27-year-old Goodness Oriete , the conversation about pollution is deeply personal . Delapidated ward at Egbema General Hospital <p> Vulnerable elderly not spared <p> For 59-year-old Margaret Vikuah , the effects of living in the shadow of gas flares are reflected in nearly every aspect of her life . <p> The cassava farmer and garri processor live in Obirikom , a community located a short distance from Okwuzi , which hosts the Obiafu-Obrikom Gas Plant . <p> The plant commenced operations in 1984 with an initial processing capacity of 270 million standard cubic feet ( mmscf ) of gas per day , equivalent to the carbon dioxide emissions from approximately 1.67 billion gallons of gasoline consumed . <p> It was upgraded to 400 mmscf/day in 1994 , making it one of the largest gas-processing plants in Nigeria . <p> Vikuah said years of standing over hot fires while processing cassava have undoubtedly taken their toll , but she believes the polluted environment itself has compounded her suffering . <p> " I constantly have itchy eyes and skin , and it has become part of my daily life , " she told Sunday PUNCH . <p> Looking across her farmland @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the environment over the years . <p> " Our atmosphere was not like this when we were growing up . Gas flaring , the burning of natural gas produced alongside crude oil , has declined from its historic peak , but Nigeria remains among the world 's largest gas-flaring countries . <p> According to data from the Gas Flare Tracker of the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency , gas flaring increased steadily from about 228 billion standard cubic feet ( Bscf @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> It then fell sharply over the next three years , reaching a decade low of 187 Bscf in 2022 before rebounding in 2023 and 2024 . By 2025 , flaring had eased again to 203.9 Bscf , remaining well below its 2019 peak . <p> A 2020 study by researchers at Rivers State University , published in the Journal of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology , found that residents of gas-flaring communities had significantly lower levels of protective antioxidants and higher markers of cellular stress than those living elsewhere , suggesting that long-term exposure may increase the risk of chronic diseases . <p> Similar concerns have emerged internationally . A landmark 2017 study by health economist Janet Currie and colleagues , published in the journal Science , analysed more than 1.1 million births in Pennsylvania and found that mothers living near natural gas extraction sites were more likely to have babies with lower birth weights and poorer health outcomes . <p> Although the study examined gas extraction rather than gas flaring specifically , it added to the broader body of evidence linking industrial air pollution with adverse maternal and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Obirikom , and Ebocha , communities where gas flares have burned for decades , those scientific findings echo concerns they have voiced for years . <p> No clear interventions <p> Despite these concerns , residents said there are few targeted interventions addressing the health effects of environmental pollution . <p> This investigation found no specialised clinics dedicated to pollution-related illnesses , while residents across several communities said they were unaware of any routine environmental health monitoring in their areas . <p> The gaps are particularly striking given Nigeria 's environmental commitments . The country belongs to the World Bank 's Global Gas Flaring Reduction Partnership , has pledged to end routine gas flaring , and participates in international methane reduction initiatives aimed at slowing global warming . <p> Methane occupies a unique place in climate science . Although it remains in the atmosphere for a shorter period than carbon dioxide , it traps far more heat . Scientists estimate that methane has more than 80 times the heat-trapping potential of carbon dioxide over 20 years , making its reduction one of the fastest ways to slow near-term global warming . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not only a climate concern but also a public health issue . @@138708778 <h> Of banditry and a shared sovereignty ( 1 ) , by Hassan Gimba <p> This piece was first published in May 2022 . It remains as pertinent today as it was then , given the worsening insecurity currently facing the country . <p> In the book : " The Impact of Banditry on Nigeria 's Security in the Fourth Republic : An Evaluation of Nigeria 's Northwest , " by Rosenje , Musharafa Olapeju ( PhD ) , and Adeniyi Oluwatobi Peter , both of the Department of Political Science , Tai Solarin University of Education , first published on 30/04/2021 , the authors posited that " Banditry is fast becoming alarming in Nigeria 's Fourth Republic to the extent that it poses a serious security threat not only to the Northwest region but to Nigeria as a whole . The level at which bandits operate within the landscape of Nigeria 's northwest has led to a spree of kidnapping , maiming of people , loss of lives , population displacements , loss of cattle , disruption of socio-economic activities and equally brought about an atmosphere of uncertainty , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the citizenry . " <p> The academics have aptly summarised what is happening in the entire country , even though their study is for the northwest and north-central regions . They said , " The pervasive banditry and its associated security threats , which have enveloped the Northwest region of Nigeria , particularly , Zamfara , Katsina , Kaduna , Sokoto and Niger states , have become a worrisome national security issue of public concern " and that " reports show the flourishing of bandit groups , whose members were seen displaying automatic weapons , terrorising herders ' settlements , farms , villages and the highways with the mission of killing people , kidnapping and pillaging cows . " <p> Their thesis went on : " It was reported that between October 2013 and March 2014 , 7000 cattle were rustled from commercial livestock farms and traditional herders in Northern Nigeria while about 330 attacks were made by bandits and 1,460 deaths were recorded between January and July 2019 . <p> " In most cases , the bandits killed and maimed the people and raped the women before dispossessing them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , while in some instances , they also kidnapped girls or women in the process ( Adeniyi , 2015 ; Yusuf , 2015 ) . Suffice to say that the Northwestern region of Nigeria encompasses seven states , namely Kano , Jigawa , Katsina , Kaduna , Zamfara , Sokoto and Kebbi . Five of these states , which are Katsina , Kaduna , Zamfara , Sokoto and Kebbi , have been most affected by the scourge of banditry . Of these five states , Kaduna , Katsina and Zamfara have been the most critical hot spots . It is , however , pertinent to note that the incidences of banditry are not limited to northwestern Nigeria . It is also prevalent in some parts of the north-central region , in states like Niger , Nasarawa , Benue and Plateau , which are equally regarded as hotbeds . " <p> Over the last decade , groups of armed bandits have kidnapped , tortured and killed hundreds of people across northwest and central Nigeria , demanding ransoms and looting citizens , rich and poor . @@138709075 <p> IN its many centuries of historical evolution , from the ancient Egyptian and Roman periods all through the French and Prussian ramifications to the British iteration of its essence , we can say without any form of exaggeration that the public service had never known the same type of challenging reality that it is currently facing in the twenty-first century . While it is true that the public service has weathered all the possible challenges it had ever encountered , from wars to famines and droughts , as well as economic recessions of all kinds , it now confronts , all across the world , all these challenges in even more severe and complicated forms . <p> Today , the world is in a polycrisis . This simply means not only that the world is confronted with unimaginable conflicts , problems and all sorts of predicaments , or that these crises and challenges are manifesting to a degree never before seen in any century . A polycrisis implies that these conflicts , crises and challenges are connected in some terribly complicated and complex ways that spell serious headaches for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ posed by climate change , for example , is not just a challenge about the inclemency of the climate alone , but how that problem aggravates agriculture , ethnic conflict , and geopolitical and geoeconomic crises everywhere across the world . Cybersecurity challenges instigate terrorism that cripples national governments and throws the world into governance crises . And that is how every other conflict and crisis makes every other conflict and crisis more troubling . <p> At the heart of all these problems , challenges , crises and predicaments of the world lies the public service that every government must depend on to confront and engage with these challenges that policies must address on behalf of the citizens . In September 2001 , the United States experienced one of the largest terrorist attacks in modern human history , and according to a commentator , a government system that " had defeated the Nazis , the Japanese and the Soviet Union was no match for a handful of terrorists . " When the World Trade Centre came tumbling down in a shower of bricks , steel and bones , it was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it did not expect and on that horrible scale . When the coronavirus hit the globe from 2019 to 2021 , it was the public services all over the world that were at the receiving end of its most brutal and traumatic charges -- hospital workers , doctors , nurses , armed forces , law enforcement officers , etc . The public servants withstood the pandemic at its most cruel points , and often without the required equipment . It was worse for every state , especially those touted as the very embodiment of infrastructural development , whose sophisticated healthcare facilities failed woefully to contain the onslaught of the ravaging virus . No government or policies or public service was prepared for the pandemic or the other crises from the Internet bubble collapse of 2000 to the US-Iran conflict of 2026 . <p> This is a very good way to commence a reflection about the state of the public service in what has been called a VUCA environment , a twenty-first-century environment that is volatile , uncertain , complex and ambiguous . A world in polycrisis is therefore a world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cherished infrastructural advancements . The VUCA environment simply implies that the public service might not always be prepared for the worst that the human mind and actions have to offer society . And the complexity of managing such a human world concerns how governments and their public services have been challenged to not only rethink their policy understanding of human progress and flourishing , but also the idea and structure of the public service that would implement these policies . <p> Given these challenging realities of the VUCA environment the public service must operate in , what questions confront the political and bureaucratic leadership in all the states across the world ? The questions are simple but significant . First , given that many of the world 's governments and public services were caught unawares and struggled with the administrative implications of the multiple crises that had befallen the world in the twenty-first century , how many more crises and upheavals are lurking in the crevices of global geopolitical relations and public governance that the public service of different states might be called upon to manage in the years ahead @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ skills and experiences of the twentieth century have become most inadequate for engaging with today 's challenges , how should the government and its public service commence the reflection and reinvention of government business in ways that fit them for today 's administration and governance ? In other words , how ought governments , especially in Africa , to reengineer the traditional Weberian public service in ways that make it resilient , pre-emptive and sufficiently agile to enable public managers to confront the VUCA environment and prepare for the decades ahead ? In what ways , for example , can the Nigerian public service become effective and efficient in handling the current polycrisis and the hard knocks that come with future crises while also learning from them ? <p> Many countries in the world today , and especially the Commonwealth of Nations , of which Nigeria is a part , inherited the Weberian bureaucracy . This is the largely hierarchical , rule-based and rational institution that determines the structural shape of the public service . This legal-rational institution promotes maximum efficiency through its insistence on compliance with rules and procedures @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the bureaucracy a stable , impersonal and officious entity designed to manage tasks in a predictable manner . The Weberian model of government business is therefore fashioned as a stabilising rather than an innovative operating system . This stifles the administrative creativity and rapid adaptation that the system requires to confront and manage disruptive challenges and innovation in the VUCA environment . <p> When the coronavirus pandemic hit the world , the Nigerian public service was able to shake its rigid characteristics and manage to adopt digital tools that enabled data-driven decision-making , administrative speed and efficiency , especially in terms of the policies that led to school closures , social distancing and other significant measures . This made for more efficient resource allocation and monitoring capacity that undergirded the data-rooted strategic communication which facilitated public trust and compliance with the measures . However , and on the downside , there was no way the system could shake its accustomed institutional inertia and poor coordination across the three tiers of government . This was compounded by under-investment , and hence insufficient , infrastructural development , especially in healthcare . This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deployment of resources and inefficient resource distribution across the country . <p> What has been the preferred framework and trend of change management for the Nigerian public service that has conditioned its administrative reforms and praxis over the years ? How , in other words , has the system pursued the reform , restructuring and reengineering of the public service institution over the years and since independence ? I will just highlight two cogent frames of change management strategies . The first is an acute reliance on global best practices , imported administrative models , external experts and consulting firms . These institutional and structural innovations and practices are usually driven by development agencies that project neoliberal paradigms , models and ideas that are developed within different contextual frameworks . Unfortunately , they generate a conception-reality gap in which institutional reforms become essentially technicist because the paradigms and models are transplanted from their source into a different and often more complex context . This makes them radically decontextualised in ways that limit or even undermine their efficacy . This is what happened with so many reform efforts , from some @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ experts and consulting firms also often operate without deep insider knowledge or collaboration . And so , this fails to generate first-hand insider perspectives on the institutional challenges and the appropriate solutions for them . The flip side of the equation is that many of the MDAs also often lack the appropriate skills and competences to efficiently deploy these universal and expert-driven practices and models in ways that enable them to adapt and adopt them to the Nigerian administrative context . <p> The second frame that has conditioned the change management plan is the deepening of institutional reform implementation through a concerted investment in training and capacity building for reform managers . These are meant as operational attempts to instigate institutional reforms and innovation through encouraging public officers and servants to learn and test new ideas and models in the context of practice . This competency-based framework manifested , for example , in the emergence of the Organisation and Methods ( O&amp;M ) unit that evolved eventually into the Management Services Office , and was replicated in the MDAs through such units as the Organisation and Management Research Unit of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what we now call the Reform Coordination Department today . Unfortunately , this deepening of the reform impulses is rather episodic because it is not intentional , systematic or part of a more comprehensive reform blueprint . Rather , it is triggered by accidental circumstances like economic crises or public criticisms . <p> All this raises for us a very important question , going forward : How can the Nigerian public service take full advantage of existing structures , systems and reform strategies in order to further stimulate and deepen the production of innovative reform solutions meant to engage and resolve both deep-seated and emerging problems ? The answer , for me , lies in context-sensitive governance reforms that aim to reconfigure public governance through an innovation-rooted reform strategy , especially through a more participatory and inclusive process that gestures towards drawing in citizens , public employees , private stakeholders and the larger society . This reform strategy demands creating national innovation systems that facilitate the collaborative relationship between public and private actors in reform networks and knowledge exchange , especially through the infusion of , say , entrepreneurial insights @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to generate " collective intelligence " that could prove to be a more reliable and resourceful methodology than unbridled reliance on pre-packaged imported models and paradigms . This can be reinforced with a proactive research and development ( R&amp;D ) backend that facilitates other methods like ethnography , including participant-observation , and design-based methods like prototyping . <p> If this analysis of the shape of the reform process is cogent , then we can multidimensionally enhance the scope of the civil service reforms by embracing public governance domains that allow innovative approaches to contribute to more social inclusion in administrative praxis . I will highlight five such domains in conclusion . One , a more expansive focus on transparent and open government through the enhancement of digital and automated access that makes the public service citizen-friendly while reducing costs . Two , strengthening citizen participation in the policy process in ways that foster trust in government and its policy actions . Three , to achieve this citizen-centred public service , the skills and competency set of public servants must necessarily be enhanced also . This implies a paradigmatic shift that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and attitude . Four , effective reform implementation demands strategic communication tools , which must be integrated into public policy instruments . Fifth and lastly , there is a need to build critical and multi-pronged collaborations that have the capacity to orient reforms towards social inclusion -- collaborations within the institutional level , between national and subnational levels , between the public service and the innovation ecosystem , between the government and the larger society , and through deepening public-private relationships . <p> *Being a presentation delivered by Olaopa , the Chairman , Federal Civil Service Commission and Professor of Public Administration , as Guest Speaker at the Nigeria Public Service Lecture marking the United Nations Public Service Day , organised by the Bureau of Public Service Reforms ( BPSR ) on June 23 , 2026 , at Nicon Luxury Hotel , Abuja.

@@138740811 <h> Explainer : Why tomato prices are surging <h> Nigeria 's consumers are facing a surge in tomato prices , with costs skyrocketing across the country . The sharp increase has left many families scrambling for alternatives , highlighting the vegetable 's growing unaffordability . <h> As of June , BusinessDay 's market data analysis shows that the fresh vegetable prices were up nearly 188 percent year to date . Across Lagos , a big basket of fresh tomatoes averages N115,000 , as compared to an average of N40,000 sold in January . <h> A small basket sells for N20,000 as against N7,000 sold in January . @@138793438 <h> PunchNG Menu : <h> When rain becomes a disaster <p> It has become a familiar ritual and , of course , an annual nightmare of sorts across Nigerian cities . Dark clouds gather and the rain begins . What ought to bring relief in the form of cooler weather and fresh air instead sends anxiety through communities . Motorists scramble for higher ground , commuters abandon vehicles , businesses shut their doors , and social media fills with videos of submerged roads , stranded families and floating cars . Within hours , another " disaster " is trending . Yet the real tragedy is that none of it is surprising or new . It happens every year . <p> One would have expected that by now , governments at all levels would have learnt from previous experiences and taken proactive measures to minimise the annual ordeal . Sadly , each rainy season seems to catch both the authorities and many residents unprepared , despite the fact that the warning signs have become as predictable as the rains themselves . <p> Why should an ordinary act of nature become an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are largely man-made . It is evident that some countries with far heavier rainfall do not grind to a halt simply because the heavens opened . Rain , in itself , rarely kills . The destruction is often caused by poor planning , blocked drainage systems , weak institutions and a culture of negligence . Rain is an act of God ; disasters are often acts of human negligence . <p> The causes of Nigeria 's flooding problem are not far-fetched . They are glaring enough for all to see . They come in the form of poor urban planning , indiscriminate construction of buildings on flood plains , uncontrolled reclamation of wetlands and road construction without adequate drainage infrastructure . Examples abound in major cities and remote communities across the country . From Lagos to Port Harcourt , Ibadan to Benin , and even smaller towns , the same ugly pattern repeats itself every rainy season . <p> The irony is that most drainage systems , where they are available , do not drain in the real sense of the word . More often than not , they have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into gutters or washed into them by floodwaters after being indiscriminately discarded elsewhere . Some drainage channels have not been desilted for years , while construction debris and silt block many others . Consequently , water that ought to flow freely has nowhere to go except onto roads , into homes and business premises . <p> It is also common to see newly completed roads without adequate attention paid to drainage . <p> In some places , drains are either too narrow to cope with heavy rainfall or terminate abruptly without proper outlets . The result is predictable : roads become rivers within minutes of a heavy rainfall . Public infrastructure that should serve the people instead becomes part of the problem . <p> Building approvals also deserve a second look . Approvals are often granted , but enforcement is weak or completely absent . This has contributed significantly to the proliferation of illegal structures and buildings erected on waterways and floodplains . In many instances , political interference prevents the removal of such structures , while compromised enforcement agencies look the other way . The consequences are borne not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ communities whenever flooding occurs . <p> The effects of these reckless practices are worsened by climate change . Rising global temperatures have contributed to more intense rainfall , rising sea levels and increasingly extreme weather conditions . Climate experts have repeatedly warned that such weather events will become more frequent and severe . However , it is important to add that climate change exposes weak systems more than strong ones . Countries with effective urban planning , resilient infrastructure and functional emergency management systems are far better equipped to cope with heavy rainfall than societies where planning has long been sacrificed on the altar of expediency . <p> When floods wreak havoc , death is often inevitable . Every year , lives are lost to collapsed buildings , overflowing rivers , electrocution and vehicles swept away by floodwaters . Families lose loved ones , while others are displaced from homes they have spent years building . <p> Beyond the tragic loss of lives , there is an enormous economic cost that is hardly ever calculated . Businesses are forced to close , with many workers unable to reach their workplaces @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Food items are destroyed , household property is damaged and vehicles are submerged beyond repair . Farmers also suffer significant losses as farmlands are washed away , thereby worsening food insecurity . These disruptions ultimately affect productivity , healthcare delivery and even insurance costs . A single afternoon of flooding can wipe out millions of naira in economic activity and impose financial burdens that linger long after the floodwaters have receded . <p> The situation is made worse by the nation 's poor emergency response system , a subject I discussed in this space last week . When streets suddenly become flooded , where are the emergency rescue boats ? Where are the flood warning systems ? How many cities have dedicated flood-response units that can be deployed within minutes ? Are emergency telephone numbers functional during storms ? Unfortunately , the answers to many of these questions are far from encouraging . Government agencies often appear only after the damage has already been done , conducting assessments , issuing statements and making promises that are quickly forgotten once the waters recede . <p> Disaster management should not begin @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ before the first drops of rain fall . Early warning systems , public education campaigns , emergency shelters and well-equipped rescue teams should all form part of a comprehensive flood management strategy rather than seasonal responses driven by media attention . <p> Citizens also share responsibility for making the environment safe , whether it rains or not . The indiscriminate dumping of refuse into drains is something that should no longer be heard of in any community in the 21st century . Building illegally is a time bomb waiting to explode . Ignoring evacuation warnings and deliberately blocking waterways are akin to sitting on a keg of gunpowder . While governments have the primary responsibility of providing infrastructure and enforcing regulations , citizens also have a duty to protect public facilities and obey environmental laws . <p> What do successful cities do differently ? They recognise that flooding is not merely an environmental issue but also an urban planning and governance issue . They invest consistently in drainage maintenance , flood forecasting , modern urban planning , strict building regulations and continuous public education . They understand that prevention is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that effective flood management is neither impossible nor miraculous . It is simply the product of good planning , political will and sustained investment . <p> Perhaps what Nigeria should be doing in practical terms includes making drainage maintenance a year-round exercise instead of waiting until the rainy season arrives . Governments should protect natural waterways , digitise flood-risk mapping , stop approving buildings on flood plains , invest substantially in modern urban drainage infrastructure , strengthen emergency response capabilities and enforce sanitation and environmental laws consistently . Also important is the need for greater collaboration among federal , state and local governments , since floodwaters do not recognise political boundaries . <p> Every rainy season , Nigerians act as though the floods have caught everyone by surprise . They have not . We have simply normalised avoidable disasters . Until governments begin to treat drainage , urban planning and flood control as essential public infrastructure rather than seasonal public relations exercises , every dark cloud will continue to trigger fear instead of relief . <p> Rain should nourish our cities , not paralyse them . It should sustain livelihoods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ national emergency , the problem is no longer the weather -- it is governance . <p> All rights reserved . @@138824581 <h> State police : Missing weapon in climate change battle ? <p> For years , Nigerians have debated the creation of state police almost exclusively through the prism of insecurity . The conversation has revolved around banditry , kidnapping , terrorism and violent crime . Yet , one crucial dimension has received scant attention : climate change . <p> Climate change is no longer merely an environmental issue . It has become a security challenge . Across Nigeria , forests are disappearing under the assault of illegal logging syndicates . Sand miners excavate riverbanks without restraint . Wetlands are reclaimed in defiance of environmental regulations . Grazing routes expand into protected ecosystems . Bush burning continues despite repeated warnings . Polluters dump hazardous wastes into rivers under the cover of darkness . <p> All these activities release greenhouse gases , destroy carbon sinks and worsen the country 's vulnerability to flooding , drought and desertification . <p> What is more , the recent statewide flooding in Lagos State has exposed another ecological reality that stares us in the face . People take advantage of rainfall to throw their domestic and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ These exacerbate the impact of the flooding on our environment . In fact , the ongoing Lagos-Calabar coastal highway is already being threatened by such callous and unpatriotic actions from citizens who should have known better . <p> The uncomfortable truth is that these environmental crimes flourish because enforcement is weak . <p> Consequently , environmental laws are often treated as mere suggestions rather than binding regulations . Climate criminals understand this weakness . <p> Illegal loggers know that the chances of being arrested deep inside remote forests are slim . Unscrupulous miners know they can abandon excavated pits after extracting valuable minerals , leaving communities exposed to erosion and deadly accidents . Developers know they can build on floodplains because local authorities possess little enforcement capacity . The boys , girls , women and men who upend their dustbins into a flowing gutter assume that no authority figure is around the corner to call them to order . <p> The result is a silent assault on Nigeria 's ecological future . And this is where state police could become an unexpected climate solution . <p> Unlike a centrally controlled @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ local geography , forests , rivers , wetlands and communities . Officers recruited from the local population would understand traditional land boundaries , seasonal environmental patterns and the identities of habitual offenders . Such familiarity makes environmental enforcement faster and more effective . <p> Imagine a state police command working closely with state ministries of environment , forestry departments , environmental health officers and local communities . Illegal chainsaw operators would be intercepted before entire forest reserves disappear . Sand mining along vulnerable riverbanks would attract immediate sanctions . Bush burning during the dry season could be prevented before wildfires spread across farmlands . And those everyday citizens waiting with their wastebaskets could be stopped before they toss their rubbish . <p> State police could also strengthen Nigeria 's commitment under international climate agreements . The country 's ambitious targets for reducing emissions and restoring degraded forests can not be achieved through policy documents alone . Every climate policy requires boots on the ground . Someone must stop illegal logging . Someone must protect mangroves . Someone must arrest those poisoning rivers with industrial waste . Today , that " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ state police could be abused by governors for political purposes . These concerns deserve serious consideration . However , the possibility of abuse should not become an excuse for institutional paralysis . Democratic societies build safeguards , not permanent excuses . Independent oversight commissions , judicial review , legislative scrutiny and constitutional limits can minimise political misuse while allowing states to address their peculiar security and environmental challenges . <p> Furthermore , environmental law enforcement creates a culture of compliance . When citizens consistently see offenders prosecuted for illegal dumping , deforestation or encroachment into protected areas , respect for environmental regulations gradually becomes part of public consciousness . Laws influence behaviour only when they are enforced . This , I think , has been the major reason behind the seeming invisibility of the environmental health officers . They lack the bite to institute deterrence . <p> Perhaps , therefore , the debate on state police requires a broader perspective . It is not merely about who carries firearms . It is about who protects forests . Who safeguards wetlands ? Who defends our rivers ? Who preserves biodiversity ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The future of Nigeria 's environmental security may depend as much on policing reform as on renewable energy , tree planting or international climate finance . <p> A nation that can not effectively protect its ecosystems can not truly claim to be fighting climate change . And perhaps that is why the conversation on state police should no longer be confined to security experts alone . Environmentalists , climate scientists , public health professionals and policymakers all deserve a seat at the table . Because in the age of climate change , every environmental offence is also a security offence . And every effective police officer may become , in a very real sense , a climate defender . <p> All rights reserved . @@138824854 <h> Breaking : Lagos named West Africa 's Most Climate-Resilient City <p> Lagos State has been ranked as the Most Climate-Resilient City in West Africa . <p> It is said to offer the most advanced and measurable climate governance among sub-national governments in the sub-continent . <p> The verdict was the outcome of the recently concluded West Africa Climate Governance Index ( WACGI ) Assessment , a comprehensive study that involved evidence-based research across all 209 sub-national governments in the 15 ECOWAS nations . <p> WACGI said its regional evaluation where Lagos and 208 other West African states were assessed combined climate-risk exposure , governance visibility , finance evidence , transparency , participation , and implementation capacity as parameters . <p> The ranking , according to WACGI , aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 13 ( Climate Action ) and SDG 17 ( Partnerships for the Goals ) . <p> The research body added that its evaluation also fell within the scope and parameters of the African Union 's Agenda 2063 aspiration for a prosperous and climate-resilient Africa . <p> With Lagos State emerging as the first in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the climate research body conferred its prestigious honour of " Grand Laureate of Climate Governance " on Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for administering the most resilient climate governance structure . <p> In an official notification letter , dated July 8 , 2026 , to the Lagos State Government , Director of Fondation Lucien Paye , Prof. Julie Peghini , congratulated Governor Sanwo-Olu for championing actions and policies aimed towards mitigating climate-related hazards and strengthening adoption in Lagos . <p> Peghini wrote : " In recognition of this achievement , we are pleased to confer upon Your Excellency and the Government of Lagos State the distinguished honour of the ' Grand Laureate of Climate Governance ' for 2026 best performing subnational government in West Africa . The formal report and the raw results datasets are publicly available on the official French Government data repository . " <p> The WACGI is a France-based climate policy and initiative centre established by the Africa Foundation ( Lucien Paye ) at Cit ? Internationale Universitaire de Paris . <p> Its mission is to advance climate governance across ECOWAS member nations . <p> This is achieved through @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Paris Agreement 's clauses . <p> Peghini said the publication reflected WACGI 's conviction that transparent , evidence-based assessment could become a powerful catalyst for institutional improvement . <p> Recognition of strong performance , she said , should inspire ranked countries , while constructive recommendations should support governments seeking to strengthen their climate governance systems . <p> The WACGI report said Nigeria , as ECOWAS 's largest economy and emissions system , enforced one of the region 's most elaborate climate governance architectures , with the county 's framework including the Climate Change Act 2021 , the National Council on Climate Change , NDC 3.0 , the Energy Transition Plan , long-term net-zero strategy and growing climate finance analysis . <p> The French body noted , however , that Nigeria faced severe climate risks across ecological zones , including coastal flooding and erosion in the South , desertification and heat in the North , riverine flooding in the Middle Belt , agricultural vulnerability , gas-flaring and oil-sector transition risks . 
@@138825079 <h> Main navigation <h> The World Is Misreading The Picture In Nigeria , By Nnamdi Prince <p> Start with the scale , because the scale alone should have ended the argument over whether this is a crisis . <p> For years , two competing stories have dominated how the world talks about violence in Nigeria . One , favored by Abuja and by many Western diplomats anxious not to inflame religious tension , describes " farmer-herder clashes " fueled by climate change and land pressure , a story of drought and desperation , not design . The other , gaining ground in Washington and in parts of the American press , describes a one-sided Christian genocide , a campaign of Islamist extermination that the Nigerian state is too weak or too complicit to stop . <p> Both stories are wrong in the same way : each is simple enough to fit a headline , and each misses what is actually happening on the ground . A new six-year compilation of violence data , drawn from Nigerian field partners and cross-checked against the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more alarming than either narrative allows : a mutation of Nigeria 's conflict from religious war into ethnic war with a religious face , one that now kills and kidnaps Muslims and Christians alike , for related but distinct reasons , while the group driving it operates with more organization and geographic reach than the jihadist movement that made Nigeria 's insecurity famous in the first place . <p> Start with the scale , because the scale alone should have ended the argument over whether this is a crisis . Between October 2019 and September 2025 , close to 79,300 people were killed in the areas of Nigeria gripped by organized violence , and nearly 35,000 more were abducted . Roughly 42,000 of the dead were civilians , killed in more than ten thousand separate attacks , an average of seven fatal incidents a day for six straight years , in a country most of the world checks in on only when a mass kidnapping trends online . <p> Then look at who is doing the killing . Boko Haram and its offshoot ISWAP , the groups most familiar to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of civilian deaths in the data set . The largest single actor was a Fulani ethnic militia , a network of armed groups drawn from Nigeria 's dominant pastoralist ethnicity , distinct from Boko Haram 's Salafi-jihadist project , responsible for 44 percent of civilians killed outright , with much of the remaining third attributed to " unidentified " armed groups that researchers believe are substantially the same actors operating under the catch-all label of " bandits . " Add those together , and one ethnic militia and its affiliates plausibly account for several times more civilian deaths than the two internationally recognized terrorist organizations combined . <p> This is the part the " farmer-herder conflict " framing can not explain and the " Christian genocide " framing does not want to hear : this militia 's violence has not stayed confined to Christian communities . Christian civilians were killed in roughly twice the numbers of Muslim civilians nationally , a gap that widens further once population size in each state is accounted for , andthe pattern in the country 's Christian-majority Middle Belt states is stark enough to support @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were Christian . But tens of thousands of Muslim civilians , overwhelmingly Hausa rather than Fulani , were killed and abducted by the same networks in the same period . By 2024 and 2025 , more Muslim civilians were being abducted in raw numbers than Christian ones . That is not what a religious extermination campaign looks like . It is what an ethnic power struggle dressed in religious language looks like , one in which " Fulani " and " Muslim " are treated as synonyms by nobody except the people writing headlines , and where being the wrong ethnicity , in the wrong village , is sometimes just as dangerous as being the wrong religion . <p> Why does this distinction matter to anyone outside Nigeria ? Because policy built on the wrong diagnosis fails . If Washington treats this purely as a story of Islamist terror , it will keep funding counter-terrorism operations against Boko Haram and ISWAP in the northeast while the deadlier violence in the North West and North Central states ; Kaduna , Zamfara , Benue , Plateau , goes largely unaddressed , because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assistance . If Abuja keeps insisting these are unavoidable " communal clashes , " it will keep sending police to farming communities after the planting season has already been disrupted and the ransoms already paid , rather than building the standing local security presence that six years of data show is glaringly absent from the areas hit hardest . And if international coverage keeps flattening this into a single-victim story , it will miss the more uncomfortable truth : that the same militias exploiting Nigeria 's weak state and its land pressures have found it strategically useful , in different places and against different communities , to let both grievancenarratives run simultaneously , because a fractured public conversation is easier to operate within than a unified one . <p> Nigeria does not need the world 's outrage pointed at the wrong target , and it does not need its own government 's euphemisms either . It needs a security response calibrated to what is actually killing people : an organized , adaptive militia structure that has quietly become deadlier than the jihadist groups the world already knows how to name @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and religious and does not resolve neatly into either category .
