@@138864131 <h> Politics or Prosecution ? The questions surrounding El-Rufai 's continued detention <p> The continued detention of Nasir El-Rufai , former Kaduna State governor , despite being charged with offences that are ordinarily bailable under Nigerian law , has opened a new front in the debate over the independence of the justice system , the treatment of opposition figures , and the boundary between legitimate prosecution and political persecution . <p> While the federal government and anti-corruption agencies insist that El-Rufai is receiving due process and fair hearing , his family , political associates and opposition parties argue that the legal process has been weaponised to keep one of the country 's most influential opposition figures out of circulation ahead of the 2027 elections . <p> The controversy has intensified following claims by Bolaji Abdullahi , the African Democratic Congress ( ADC ) spokesman , that the ruling All Progressives Congress ( APC ) intends to keep El-Rufai in detention until after the next general election . <p> " What I can tell you is that the thinking within the ADC is that the APC government has concluded that they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " Abdullahi said during a Channels Television interview . <p> At the centre of the dispute is not whether El-Rufai should face trial . Even opposition figures have largely acknowledged that anyone accused of criminal conduct should answer questions before the courts . Rather , the debate is whether the bail conditions imposed in multiple cases are so stringent that they effectively amount to detention by another name . <p> The cases against El-Rufai <p> El-Rufai is facing separate prosecutions in Kaduna and Abuja . <p> The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission ( ICPC ) has charged him over alleged abuse of office , fraud , money laundering and procurement-related offences arising from his tenure as governor of Kaduna State . <p> Among the allegations is the approval of a contract for the procurement , survey planning , final design and installation of a CCTV surveillance system in Kaduna metropolis at a revised cost of N8.68 billion . <p> The wire-tapping case arose after El-Rufai claimed during a television interview that he had listened to an intercepted conversation allegedly involving the NSA discussing plans for his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Cybercrimes Act and the Nigerian Communications Act relating to unlawful interception of communications , failure to report an interception and compromising national security through the use of technical equipment . <p> The strongest argument advanced by El-Rufai 's supporters concerns the conditions attached to his bail . <p> In the federal case , the court granted him bail in the sum of N100 million . However , one surety must be a Grade Level 17 federal civil servant with property in either Maitama or Asokoro , two of Abuja 's most expensive districts . The surety must also provide an original certificate of occupancy alongside evidence of tax payments and salary records . <p> The court further ordered El-Rufai to report to the DSS every month . His lawyers sought a variation of the conditions , arguing that they were excessive and difficult to satisfy . Justice Joyce Abdulmalik declined the request , holding that qualified civil servants who meet the conditions exist . <p> In Kaduna , another court reportedly required two sureties with properties worth N200 million each , alongside attestation from the Kaduna State Traditional Council @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ former governor 's wives , efforts to fulfil the conditions encountered obstacles . <p> " The Traditional Council would not give that attestation , " she said during an Arise Television interview . <p> She also alleged that the Kaduna State Land Registry was shut during efforts to verify property documents required for the bail process . The government has not publicly accepted these claims . <p> The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that bail conditions should ensure the attendance of an accused person during trial . However , courts have also warned against imposing terms so onerous that they effectively deny bail . <p> What makes El-Rufai 's situation unusual is not necessarily the monetary value involved but the combination of requirements . The insistence on Grade Level 17 officers with properties in specific elite districts and additional institutional attestations has fuelled claims that the conditions are exceptionally difficult to satisfy . <p> " Look at what is happening with my brother , Mallam Nasir el-Rufai . He is currently in custody , and the requirements for his release are incredibly difficult , " Sanusi Lamido Sanusi , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Hausa . <p> The treatment of other high-profile defendants offers a mixed picture . <p> Ayodele Fayose , former Ekiti governor , who faced money laundering charges before the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission ( EFCC ) , was granted bail and released after meeting court conditions despite the scale of allegations against him . He was later discharged and acquitted by the court . <p> Orji Uzor Kalu , former Abia governor , was granted bail during his corruption trial and remained free for much of the proceedings before his eventual conviction , which was later nullified by the Supreme Court . <p> Sambo Dasuki , former national security adviser , charged for alleged $2.1B arms procurement fraud during late Muhammadu Buhari 's administration spent years in detention despite multiple court orders granting him bail . Human rights groups described his case as one of the most controversial examples of prolonged pre-trial detention in Nigeria 's democratic history . <p> Godwin Emefiele , former Central Bank governor , under prosecution by the current administration was also held for extended periods while contesting bail conditions in multiple courts . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ charges is not unprecedented , it has often attracted allegations of political interference and selective justice . <p> While there is no judicial precedent of a high-profile individual being criminally prosecuted for phone wiretapping , the offense is however bailable . <p> The anti-corruption agency alleged that the doctor made false statements relating to a court-approved medical visit and accused El-Rufai of receiving political associates during what was supposed to be a medical consultation . <p> The agency argued that such conduct violated the court 's order . <p> Supporters of the former governor , however , view the arrest as further evidence of an aggressive prosecutorial strategy designed to limit his political activities . <p> Politics in the background <p> Whether acknowledged or not , the political context is impossible to ignore . <p> El-Rufai is no ordinary defendant . Since leaving the APC and aligning with the ADC-led opposition coalition , he has become one of President Bola Tinubu 's fiercest critics . <p> His speeches , interviews and organisational role within the opposition have made him a key figure in preparations for the 2027 election . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ through a political lens . <p> For ADC leaders , the timing and cumulative effect of the prosecutions suggest an effort to weaken the opposition . For the government , the argument is straightforward : criminal allegations should not disappear simply because an accused person becomes politically influential . <p> Is the government being fair ? <p> The answer depends largely on which standard is applied . <p> On one hand , El-Rufai has been charged before competent courts , given access to lawyers and allowed to challenge the cases against him . @@138883349 <h> Migratory birds and crisis of ecological neglect <p> The alarming revelation by conservationists that more than 40 per cent of migratory bird species worldwide are now in decline should worry governments , environmentalists and citizens alike . Beyond the beauty of birds in flight lies a deeper ecological crisis that signals the deteriorating health of the planet itself . <p> Migratory birds are among nature 's greatest wonders . Every year , millions of birds travel thousands of kilometres across continents and oceans , linking ecosystems , seasons and communities in an extraordinary cycle of survival . Yet , this timeless natural phenomenon is increasingly under threat . <p> The warning by the Chief Executive Officer of BirdLife International , Martin Harper , is not merely about birds disappearing from the skies . It is about the collapse of ecological systems that sustain agriculture , water resources , biodiversity and ultimately human existence . <p> Migratory birds are vital indicators of environmental health because they depend on interconnected ecosystems spread across countries and continents . When their numbers decline , it reflects widespread habitat destruction , pollution , climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agricultural systems benefit from birds that naturally control crop-destroying pests , reducing dependence on harmful chemicals . Wetlands and coastal ecosystems frequented by migratory species also provide flood control , water purification and climate resilience for millions of people . <p> The yearly observance of World Migratory Bird Day , celebrated during May and October to align with migration seasons in both hemispheres , is therefore more than a ceremonial event . It is a reminder that humanity shares a common ecological destiny . The migration routes , known as global flyways , connect breeding grounds , feeding habitats and seasonal refuges across the world . These flyways represent some of the most delicate ecological corridors on Earth . <p> Among the most significant is the African -- Eurasian Flyway , which links Africa with Europe and parts of Asia . Every year , countless birds leave the warmth of Africa and travel northward to breed . However , the survival of these species increasingly depends on whether wetlands remain intact , forests are preserved and coastlines protected from reckless development . <p> Unfortunately , human activities are rapidly breaking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ urban expansion , industrial pollution is contaminating water bodies , illegal hunting persists in many regions , while climate change is altering migration patterns and food availability . Coastal degradation , desertification and uncontrolled infrastructural projects continue to destroy habitats essential to migratory birds . The extinction of the Slender-billed Curlew , referenced by conservationists , is a painful reminder of what happens when humanity fails to act in time . Once widespread across parts of Europe and Asia , the species disappeared largely because of habitat destruction and hunting pressure . Its extinction should serve as a global warning that many other migratory species may soon follow unless urgent interventions are implemented . <p> Africa occupies a strategic position in global bird migration networks . As Dr Paul Matiku of Nature Kenya rightly observed , the continent lies at the centre of some of the world 's major flyways . This places enormous responsibility on African governments and institutions to protect wetlands , forests , rivers and coastal ecosystems that support migratory species . <p> Nigeria , in particular , can not afford to remain indifferent . The country @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , including the Hadejia-Nguru wetlands , the Niger Delta mangroves and coastal lagoons around Lagos . Yet many of these ecosystems face severe threats from oil pollution , sand mining , urban encroachment , deforestation and weak environmental enforcement . The shrinking of wetlands in northern Nigeria due to climate stress and poor water management has already affected biodiversity and local livelihoods . In coastal areas , unchecked dredging and land reclamation projects continue to destroy habitats that birds depend on for feeding and nesting . Environmental policies often exist only on paper , while enforcement agencies remain underfunded and politically constrained . <p> The irony is that protecting migratory birds also protects people . Conservationists are correct in emphasising that healthy flyways contribute to cleaner water , stronger food systems , flood prevention and climate resilience . The destruction of wetlands , for instance , not only threatens birds but also exposes communities to flooding , erosion and water scarcity . Biodiversity conservation is therefore not a luxury reserved for environmental activists ; it is a practical necessity for economic survival and public welfare . There is also an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Ecotourism centred on bird watching generates billions of dollars globally and supports thousands of jobs . Countries that preserve biodiversity attract researchers , tourists and conservation funding . Africa possesses immense potential in this regard , yet environmental neglect continues to undermine such opportunities . <p> The forthcoming Global Flyways Summit co-hosted by BirdLife International and Nature Kenya is therefore timely . Bringing together experts from science , policy , finance , business and civil society offers an opportunity to move beyond rhetoric towards measurable action . However , conferences and declarations alone will not save migratory birds unless governments demonstrate political will . <p> Public awareness is another vital component . Schools , media organisations and community groups should intensify environmental education to help citizens understand the value of migratory birds and biodiversity conservation . Indigenous knowledge systems that traditionally protected ecosystems should also be recognised and strengthened . <p> Ultimately , the decline of migratory birds is warning signal humanity can not ignore . Nature operates through interconnected systems , and when one part collapses , the consequences spread far beyond wildlife . <p> The disappearance of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ agriculture , economies , health and climate stability . <p> The world still has an opportunity to reverse these trends , but time is running out . Protecting migratory birds requires collective global responsibility because flyways transcend political borders . No nation can succeed alone if neighbouring countries continue to destroy habitats and weaken conservation efforts . <p> Humanity must decide whether future generations will inherit a world still alive with the seasonal movement of birds across continents , or a silent planet diminished by environmental neglect . The choice should not be difficult .

@@138930944 <h> The Lagos floods <p> FOR many residents of Lagos , the past few weeks have been an ordeal . Homes have been inundated , businesses temporarily shut , vehicles stranded , children ferried to school by boats , and countless families forced to wade through floodwaters simply to go about their daily lives . Communities such as Lekki , Awoyaya , Bogije , Lakowe , Agungi , Amuwo-Odofin , Yaba , Ikoyi and several other parts of the metropolis have once again experienced the now familiar disruption that accompanies heavy rainfall in Nigeria 's economic capital . Recent reports also indicate that businesses were forced to close , transport networks were disrupted , and the government has ordered additional dredging and drainage interventions following the flooding . Unfortunately , there is little about this scene that is new . <p> Every rainy season , Lagos braces for flooding . Every rainy season , residents count their losses . Every rainy season , government agencies explain the causes and promise improvements . Then the rains return , and the cycle is repeated . This cycle can not become the accepted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reality : flooding in Lagos is not simply evidence of governmental failure . It is the product of geography , climate , demography , urbanisation and human behaviour interacting simultaneously . Lagos occupies low-lying coastal terrain bordered by the Atlantic Ocean and an extensive lagoon system . During periods of intense rainfall and high lagoon or tidal levels , stormwater naturally drains more slowly . Climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme rainfall events , while rising sea levels further complicate drainage in coastal cities . Similar challenges are confronting other West African coastal cities , including Accra in Ghana , where recent floods have also caused deaths and extensive destruction . <p> Recognising these realities , however , should never become an excuse for resignation . Natural hazards become disasters largely because societies fail to prepare adequately for them . The Lagos State government deserves credit for maintaining one of the country 's more active environmental ministries . It has continued drainage maintenance , issued advance flood warnings , removed illegal structures from drainage setbacks , approved dredging of additional drainage channels , and commenced longer-term flood-control projects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the scale of the challenge now demands even bolder thinking . Flood management must shift decisively from emergency response to resilience building . <p> The objective is to build a city that can absorb heavy rainfall without paralysing daily life . That requires stricter enforcement against structures obstructing natural waterways and drainage corridors . Buildings that block the natural movement of water ultimately endanger entire communities . Difficult as such enforcement may be , allowing these obstructions to remain only guarantees greater future losses . It also requires a fundamental rethinking of urban growth . Lagos continues to attract hundreds of thousands of new residents every year , many settling in flood-prone areas because that is where affordable housing exists . As population pressure intensifies , impermeable concrete increasingly replaces natural land surfaces , leaving rainwater with fewer places to infiltrate the ground and greater volumes flowing rapidly into already overwhelmed drainage systems . Urban planning must therefore become part of flood policy . Government should actively discourage new residential developments in highly vulnerable floodplains while creating attractive alternatives elsewhere . This is where neighbouring South-West states have an important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , residents should increasingly be able to live in Ogun , Oyo , Osun or other nearby states while commuting conveniently into Lagos . Such regional integration would reduce pressure on Lagos while stimulating balanced economic development across the South-West . <p> Similarly , the government should accelerate the development of higher-elevation growth corridors such as parts of Badagry , while ensuring that new communities are designed as genuinely climate-resilient smart cities rather than simply expanding today 's vulnerabilities into tomorrow 's suburbs . The city must also rethink how stormwater reaches the lagoon . As rainfall intensity increases , drainage infrastructure designed decades ago may no longer possess sufficient capacity . Continuous expansion , modernisation and engineering redesign of drainage channels will become unavoidable if Lagos is to remain functional as climate patterns evolve . Equally important is the role of citizens . No drainage system can function effectively if it serves as a refuse dump . As climate risks intensify , resilience -- not reaction -- must become the organising principle of urban governance . More than 10 per cent of the lost sleep was attributed to climate change , driven largely by fossil fuel emissions and deforestation . <p> According to the analysis , this is the first study to quantify the number of sleep hours lost because of climate change by combining climate attribution science with research on the effects of heat on sleep . <p> The report found that climate change-related sleep loss has at least doubled since the early 1970s in almost every city analysed . <p> Residents of cities across the Middle East recorded the highest levels of climate-related sleep loss , while southern India , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Niger and Burkina Faso , also experienced significant sleep disruption . <p> According to the report , people in some West African cities lost more than 65 hours of sleep annually due to high nighttime temperatures , with about 10 to 11 of those hours directly linked to climate change . <p> Climate experts warned that rising overnight temperatures make it harder for the body to cool down and recover from daytime heat , increasing the risk of cardiovascular diseases , stroke , poor mental health , reduced productivity and premature death . <p> The report also noted that infants , older adults , pregnant women and low-income populations are among the most vulnerable because of limited access to cooling systems and quality housing . <p> Climate Central 's Vice President for Science , Dr Kristina Dahl , said the findings highlight another hidden consequence of global warming . <p> " This analysis reveals how climate change is translating into measurable hours of lost sleep for people around the world . @@139022997 <h> How Clean Energy Benefits Agriculture And Environment <p> Did you know that how we produce and consume food can have a huge impact on the environment ? Some of these environmental impacts can include water pollution , carbon and other harmful greenhouse gas emissions , deforestation , pesticide toxicity , biodiversity loss , and so on . <p> There is , therefore , an urgent need for us to reexamine the ways in which we produce and consume food , in an effort to reduce negative impacts on our environment , economy and health , as well as to build resilience against shocks like economic disruptions . <p> So , how can we attempt to build a food system that has minimal negative impacts on the environment , and that would be far more resilient to future economic shocks ? One way we can do this is by shifting towards climate-smart agriculture -- by using renewable energy sources in our agricultural production processes . <p> What is Renewable Energy ? Renewable Energy is energy derived from natural sources that are replenished at a higher rate than they are consumed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sources that are constantly being replenished . Renewable Energy Sources are plentiful and all around us . A few common sources of renewable energy include the following : Solar Energy ; Wind Energy ; Geothermal Energy ; Hydropower ; Ocean Energy ; and Bioenergy ( produced from a variety of organic materials , called biomass , such as wood , charcoal , dung and other manures for heat and power production , and agricultural crops for liquid biofuels ) . <p> However , it is important to note that although biofuels , such as ethanol and bio-diesel are often portrayed as sustainable alternatives to fuel , the crops used to produce these fuels ( such as corn and rapeseed ) can occupy a great expanse of land , which could otherwise be used for things like food production , re-wilding and carbon storage . <p> Fossil fuels -- coal , oil and gas -- on the other hand , are non-renewable resources that take hundreds of millions of years to form . Fossil fuels , when burned to produce energy , cause harmful greenhouse gas emissions , such as carbon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ creates far lower emissions than burning fossil fuels . Therefore , to address growing concerns about global warming and climate change , the time has now come for us to make a transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy ! Furthermore , renewables are now cheaper in most countries , and can even generate three times more jobs than fossil fuels ! <p> Nowadays , it is very common for farmers and other agricultural experts to use Nitrogen-based fertilizers in their agricultural production processes . One of the key ingredients of Nitrogen-based fertilizer is ammonia . Ammonia is usually produced using fossil fuels , and fossil fuels , including coal , oil and natural gas , are the primary drivers of global climate change . Therefore , in order to mitigate the worst impacts of global warming , societies are actively shifting away from fossil fuels in favour of renewable energy systems and cleaner industrial processes . <p> Have you heard about " green ammonia " ? " Green Ammonia " refers to ammonia that is produced using renewable energy sources , including sunshine and wind . " Green Ammonia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fuels . So , it is now possible to produce homegrown nitrogen-based fertilizer consisting of " green ammonia , " when the sun shines and the wind blows . <p> According to an article titled : " How the world can avoid millions going hungry when supply chains collapse , " which I read up from the Oxford Martin School website ( oxfordmartin. ox.co.uk ) , and which was originally published in The Conversation ( www.theconversation.com ) , an independent news website : " The first green ammonia plants are now being constructed in sunny places such as Chile , Morocco , and Australia . " The article went on to state that although it is an expensive switch from fossil fuels to " green ammonia " , the declining cost of renewable energy sources combined with wildly fluctuating fuel prices could soon make it a more competitive and secure alternative . However , as the article further stated : " A successful transition from fossil fuels to " green ammonia " will depend on sustained commitment ( and investment ) from governments . " <p> Building a more resilient @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ like changing our diet , switching our type of fuels , and changing our types of fertilizers takes time . It will involve trade-offs as well as considerable governmental commitment/input , and commercial will . None of that is easy to achieve . @@139022999 <p> Before examining the advantages of non-kinetic strategies over kinetic ones , it is necessary to understand the underlying drivers of insurgency and banditry in Northern Nigeria . Among the most frequently cited factors are religious extremism and poverty . <p> To better understand how these factors influence vulnerable individuals and communities , I examined available research and historical experiences from societies that have faced similar crises . <p> The evidence suggests that religion and poverty do not , by themselves , cause kidnapping , banditry , or terrorism . Rather , they serve as accelerants and recruitment tools . In environments characterised by weak governance , limited economic opportunities , social exclusion , and easy access to weapons , these factors combine to create conditions that foster insecurity . <p> Notably , many of these conditions have existed in Nigeria since the return to multi-party democracy in 1999 . <p> Therefore , while the current wave of insecurity can not be attributed solely to the incumbent administration , it remains the responsibility of the government to develop and implement sustainable solutions . What began as an isolated criminal enterprise has evolved into a thriving industry . A single successful kidnapping operation can generate income equivalent to what a farmer may earn over an entire decade . <p> Even bandits who previously relied on cattle rustling as their primary source of income now find kidnapping more attractive . Abducting schoolchildren , teachers , or travellers often yields enormous ransom payments while exposing perpetrators to less risk than attempting to sell stolen cattle in regulated markets where they can be identified and arrested . <p> As experience has shown , economic desperation lowers the threshold for violence . <p> Another important factor is the loss of state legitimacy . <p> When governments fail to provide essential services such as schools , healthcare facilities , roads , and other basic infrastructure , public trust inevitably erodes . For many years , this was the reality in large parts of Northern Nigeria . In response , successive governments have sought to bridge these gaps through initiatives such as the establishment of Almajiri schools and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the alarming number of out-of-school children , estimated at between 15 and 20 million . <p> While these interventions are commendable , they came after decades of neglect . During such periods of state absence , criminal groups often step in to provide alternative forms of authority and protection , thereby winning the loyalty of local populations . <p> Land and resource conflicts also stem from poverty , climate change , and desertification . Competition over farmland , water resources , and grazing routes has intensified across Northern Nigeria and the wider Sahel region , becoming a significant driver of violence and banditry . <p> The critical point , however , is that poverty alone does not create terrorists . While it makes individuals more vulnerable to recruitment , an ideology , criminal enterprise , or extremist network is usually required to channel that vulnerability into organised violence . <p> ( 2 ) Religion : The Justification And Mobilising Force <p> Contrary to popular belief , religion itself is rarely the root cause of insecurity . Rather , the problem arises when religion is weaponised . <p> One of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organisations frequently manipulate religious texts to portray violence as a " holy war , " a " defense of the faith , " or a process of " purification . " Such narratives provide moral cover for violent acts and make compromise more difficult . <p> Religion can also be exploited to create an " us versus them " mentality . By defining identity primarily through religious affiliation , extremist groups establish clear distinctions between perceived allies and enemies . <p> For example , Boko Haram 's ideological message has often been summarised as " Western education is forbidden . " In some areas , criminal groups have sought to frame conflicts through a Christian-versus-Muslim lens , particularly in disputes involving farmers and herders , thereby mobilising vulnerable populations along sectarian lines . <p> Religious institutions , schools , preachers , and networks can also be exploited as recruitment and mobilisation platforms . Shared beliefs often foster strong group cohesion , making it easier for extremist organisations to attract and retain followers . <p> Furthermore , religious charities , donations , and transnational networks can sometimes be manipulated to provide @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Leaders of such movements frequently invoke divine authority to justify their actions and reinforce their influence over followers . <p> The indictment of terrorism sponsored recently identified by the authorities and USA and shared with Nigerian authorities is amongst the right decisions aimed at tightening the noose around insecurity in Nigeria in a bid to end it in non-kinetic ways . <p> Having said that , religion alone does not generate insecurity . <p> There are deeply religious societies around the world that experience little or no religious insurgency . Likewise , poverty alone does not automatically produce criminality . Many poor countries have relatively low levels of terrorism and organised violence . <p> More often than not , a third factor is present : weak state institutions , corruption , the proliferation of weapons , or political actors who exploit poverty and religious identity in pursuit of personal , ethnic , or political agendas . <p> The armed conflicts in Libya and surrounding areas have made arms and ammunition more easily accessible even as the recent report that foreigners were sighted amongst the bandits recently operating in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ What Can Reduce Insecurity ? <p> A quick research that I conducted on the matter suggests that the most effective long-term antidotes to insecurity are economic development , job creation , access to education , and accelerated infrastructure development . These measures shrink the recruitment pool available to criminal organisations and extremist groups . <p> Equally important is good governance , underpinned by responsive policing , effective courts , and reliable public services . These institutions help restore public confidence and reduce the appeal of criminal alternatives . <p> In many respects , these are among the objectives President Bola Tinubu 's administration is pursuing through increased allocation of funds to state governments owing to the growing revenue accruing to the federal government arising from petrol subsidy removal , investments in infrastructure- roads , air and sea ports , the National Education Loan Fund ( NELFUND ) democratizing education , and ongoing efforts to strengthen state and local policing mechanisms that largely disappeared following the military coup of 1966 . <p> There is also a critical religious dimension to the solution . Credible religious leaders must be empowered to challenge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ groups to recruit followers . By separating religion from the politics of violence , clerics can help inoculate communities against radicalisation . <p> The Case For Non-Kinetic Strategies <p> The successful rescue of the Oriire schoolchildren and teachers demonstrates the effectiveness of non-kinetic approaches to insecurity . <p> By disrupting the finances , intelligence networks , and logistical structures of criminal groups , as was done in the Oriire case , security agencies can achieve outcomes that military force alone may not deliver . <p> The lesson is clear : reliance solely on kinetic measures -- the use of armed force -- can not resolve insecurity . Without complementary non-kinetic measures such as economic development , effective governance , and counter-radicalisation initiatives , the problem merely shifts from one location to another . As Americans often say , it amounts to " kicking the can down the road . " <p> This is the central argument I advance in my new book , ' The Imperative of State Police in Nigeria ' , scheduled for public presentation in Abuja on September 10 . <p> Poverty supplies the manpower for criminal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and narrative . State weakness creates the operating space , particularly within the vast ungoverned forests that exist across the country . <p> State policing is not a complete solution , but it is undoubtedly part of the answer . Local police officers understand the terrain , speak the language , know the communities , and work closely with traditional rulers , religious leaders , and local stakeholders to disrupt recruitment before it begins . <p> While state police alone can not eliminate poverty-driven or religiously motivated insecurity , it would represent a powerful counterforce . <p> Chibok And Oriire : A Tale Of Two Security Responses <p> At this point , it is useful to contrast the abduction of the Chibok schoolgirls with the recent Oriire kidnapping . <p> Although the Chibok abduction occurred in 2014 , the broader point remains valid . More than a decade later , to be specific a dozen years after , several of the girls remain unaccounted for despite extensive military operations . <p> That is probably due to late intervention or lack of concerted efforts or non-synergistic action of all the relevant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , enabling the bandits to move the victims beyond the confines of Nigeria and likely sold into slavery as they had threatened . <p> By contrast , the Oriire pupils and teachers , abducted on May 15 , were released on July 10 after less than two months in captivity . <p> According to the account provided by Army spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Danjuma Jonah Danjuma , the rescue operation involved isolating the kidnappers , restricting their movement , disrupting their supply routes , and exerting pressure on their support networks . These measures appear to have complemented conventional military operations and contributed significantly to the successful outcome . <p> The Next Challenge : Prevention <p> While the successful rescue of the Oriire victims provides valuable lessons , it remains only one piece of a much larger puzzle . <p> Rescuing hostages after an abduction has occurred is important . At the time , Nigeria was emerging as a regional power , funding peacekeeping missions , supporting liberation movements in Africa and providing assistance to neighbouring countries . <p> The country was so wealthy that General Yakubu Gowon was famously quoted as saying that Nigeria 's problem was not money , but how to spend it . <p> Five decades later , that statement reads like a relic from another era . <p> Nigeria @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and development plans . According to the Debt Management Office , the country 's public debt rose to N159.28 trillion by the end of 2025 . The 2026 federal budget earmarks about N15.8 trillion for debt servicing alone , an amount that exceeds the combined capital budgets of several key sectors . <p> The transformation from creditor to debtor raises a troubling question : what happened ? <p> The answer lies not in a single event but in decades of missed opportunities . <p> The oil boom of the 1970s created enormous wealth , but it also encouraged a dangerous dependence on crude oil . Agriculture , which had been Nigeria 's leading export sector before oil , gradually declined . Manufacturing struggled to compete , while successive governments relied increasingly on oil revenues to fund public spending . <p> When global oil prices collapsed in the early 1980s , the weakness of the economy became exposed . Government revenues fell sharply , foreign exchange earnings dwindled and borrowing began to replace oil income as a source of financing . <p> Rather than use the crisis to diversify the economy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oil . Periods of high oil prices brought temporary relief , but they were often accompanied by higher government spending rather than long-term investments that could generate sustainable growth . <p> The return to democracy in 1999 offered another opportunity for economic renewal . Rising oil prices during the 2000s generated billions of dollars in additional revenues . In 2005 , Nigeria secured debt relief from the Paris Club , eliminating about $18 billion in external debt and providing what many economists described as a fresh start . <p> The problem was not necessarily the loans themselves . Every major economy borrows . The critical issue is how borrowed funds are used . <p> In countries where debt finances productive infrastructure , industrial expansion or technological development , borrowing can stimulate growth and generate the resources needed for repayment . In Nigeria , however , the outcomes have often been less visible . <p> Despite decades of borrowing , many roads remain in poor condition , electricity supply is inadequate , public schools are underfunded and healthcare infrastructure remains weak . While some debt-financed projects have improved transportation and connectivity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Corruption has also played a significant role . <p> For years , anti-corruption agencies have uncovered cases involving billions of naira in stolen public funds . Yet convictions are often delayed , assets are not fully recovered and many high-profile cases end with plea bargains . The perception that public officials can loot state resources with limited consequences has undermined confidence in governance . <p> A growing share of government revenue is spent servicing existing debts rather than building new infrastructure or expanding social services . At the same time , inflation , unemployment and poverty continue to affect millions of Nigerians . Citizens are increasingly asking why rising public debt has not translated into a comparable improvement in living standards . <p> Yet debt is only a symptom of a deeper problem . <p> The real issue is the inability of the economy to generate sufficient revenue outside oil , combined with persistent inefficiencies in public spending . Nigeria 's population has grown from about 56 million in 1970 to more than 230 million today , placing enormous pressure on infrastructure , education , healthcare and employment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has vast oil and gas reserves , fertile agricultural land , a large domestic market and a youthful population . What has been lacking is the consistent policy framework needed to convert those assets into broad-based prosperity . <p> Nigeria 's journey from lender to borrower offers a lesson in economic management . Natural resources alone do not guarantee development . Wealth must be invested productively , institutions must be strengthened and public resources must be managed transparently . <p> Half a century ago , Nigeria was helping to fund global financial institutions . Today , it relies on many of those same institutions for support . <p> Taofeek Oyedokun is a correspondent at BusinessDay with years of experience reporting on political economy , public policy , migration , environment/climate change , and social justice . @@139137044 <h> Lagos must treat annual flooding as a long-term existential threat <p> Across the world , several coastal cities face projections that large parts of their urban areas could be permanently submerged by water by 2050 . Many have spent decades investing in flood-control systems , coastal protection and climate adaptation , but still regard rising sea levels as one of their greatest long-term threats . <p> Climate modelling and elevation data from organisations such as Climate Central show that major cities including Jakarta in Indonesia , Mumbai in India , Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam , Bangkok in Thailand , Shanghai in China , Alexandria in Egypt , New Orleans and Miami in America face increasing risks from rising sea levels and are projected to either have large areas submerged or chronically flooded by 2050 . <p> Despite their different geographies , they all recognise flooding as a strategic threat requiring continuous investment rather than seasonal intervention . <p> However , Lagos , Africa 's largest coastal city and Nigeria 's commercial capital , faces similar risks but continues to respond to flooding largely as a seasonal emergency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change in approach , today 's annual floods may become tomorrow 's irreversible urban crisis in Lagos . <p> These threats result from the combined effects of climate change and human-induced environmental degradation . Scientists describe the situation as a " deadly paradox " , in which land is sinking while sea levels continue to rise . Excessive groundwater extraction , expanding concrete infrastructure and collapsing sediment layers are causing many coastal cities to subside , even as global warming raises sea levels through melting ice sheets and the thermal expansion of oceans . Meanwhile , rapid urbanisation has destroyed natural flood buffers such as mangrove forests , wetlands and river deltas , making coastal cities more vulnerable to permanent inundation . <p> Lagos is already exhibiting many of the same warning signs confronting these vulnerable coastal cities . <p> Flooding has become an annual feature of life in Lagos . As a low-lying coastal megacity , the city experiences recurrent flooding throughout the rainy season , which runs from March to December under the West African monsoon cycle . The highest risk usually occurs between July and October , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and frequently submerges major roads and residential communities . Although the brief " August Break " temporarily reduces rainfall , heavy downpours soon return , increasing both flash and riverine flooding . <p> In some years , water releases from the Oyan Dam further worsen flooding in parts of the Lagos mainland . According to the National Emergency Management Agency ( NEMA ) and the Lagos State Ministry of Environment , the most vulnerable areas include Lekki , Victoria Island , Lagos Island , Ikeja , Surulere , Agege , Alimosho , Ikorodu , Isheri , Owode and Ketu , where flooding repeatedly disrupts homes , businesses and critical infrastructure . <p> The sad reality for Lagosians is that , despite government budget allocations exceeding ? 106 billion for drainage infrastructure , very little appears to have changed in the city 's ability to manage flooding effectively . Every rainy season , thousands of residents watch floodwaters invade their homes , particularly on Lagos Island , destroying properties worth millions of naira , displacing families and disrupting livelihoods . Floodwaters regularly submerge vehicles on major highways , while some communities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ problem extends beyond the Island , with overflowing drains and impassable roads disrupting communities across the mainland . <p> This has become an annual cycle of destruction in which reactive rather than preventive responses fail to protect lives , property and critical infrastructure . The persistence of the crisis raises serious questions about whether Lagos has a credible long-term flood management strategy . The concern is even more urgent given projections that about 1.4 million residents could be at risk and that flooding could cost the city an estimated US$40 billion by 2050 if inadequate long-term infrastructure planning continues . <p> Even cities facing similar flood risks are investing in long-term engineering and nature-based solutions to reduce their vulnerability . In New Orleans , authorities have constructed massive surge barriers , reinforced levees and one of the world 's largest pumping systems to keep floodwaters out and rapidly remove excess water . Shanghai has pioneered the " Sponge City " approach by replacing impermeable surfaces with porous pavements , rain gardens and wetlands that absorb stormwater , while deep drainage tunnels , intelligent floodgates and extensive waterways redirect and store @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ installed industrial stormwater pumping stations and backflow preventers that prevent seawater from flowing back into streets during high tides , complemented by the elevation of roads , seawalls and buildings to improve the city 's resilience against chronic flooding . <p> Lagos should learn from these experiences by adapting proven technologies and policies to its own environment . Beyond engineering , the city needs a genuine long-term flood resilience strategy . Urban planning should discourage development in high-risk flood zones while restoring wetlands and other natural flood buffers . Drainage infrastructure must be expanded and maintained using modern hydrological modelling rather than reacting after disasters occur . Early-warning systems , emergency evacuation planning and stronger coordination between state agencies should become permanent features of urban governance , supported by transparent project monitoring and public accountability for implementation . <p> Annual flooding should no longer be treated as an unavoidable consequence of heavy rainfall . It is an increasingly predictable risk whose consequences will become more severe if current patterns continue . @@139168605 <h> Nigeria can not defeat climate change without investing in water science <p> ByMohammad Danasabe Umar <p> Mon , 20 Jul 2026 4:18:48 WAT <p> For millions of Nigerians , climate change is not an abstract environmental issue but a daily reality of rising temperatures , floods , droughts , shrinking water sources , contaminated groundwater and increasingly unpredictable rainfall . <p> In Nigeria , climate change is fundamentally a water crisis . <p> This distinction matters because it changes how we think about solutions . If climate change manifests itself largely through water , then Nigeria 's response can not depend solely on environmental campaigns or emergency relief . It must begin with understanding water itself -- how it moves , where it is stored , how it is changing and how those changes affect agriculture , public health , energy production and national security . <p> That understanding comes from science . <p> Unfortunately , scientific capacity rarely occupies the centre of Nigeria 's climate conversation . Every rainy season follows a familiar pattern . Floods devastate communities , roads collapse , bridges are washed away and thousands @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emergency funds released and promises made to prevent similar disasters in the future . Yet when the waters recede , attention shifts elsewhere until the next catastrophe arrives . <p> This cycle of reaction has become one of Nigeria 's greatest weaknesses in confronting climate change . <p> Across the world , countries that have successfully reduced climate vulnerability have invested patiently in research institutions capable of generating evidence for public policy . The Netherlands transformed centuries of experience with flooding into one of the world 's most sophisticated systems of water management through sustained investment in engineering , hydrology and specialised education . Its globally admired flood-control infrastructure did not emerge overnight ; it was built upon decades of scientific research , institutional continuity and political commitment . <p> South Africa offers another instructive example . Through the work of its Water Research Commission , scientific findings routinely inform national decisions on water security , agriculture , sanitation and resource management . The country 's experience demonstrates that research institutions are not peripheral bureaucracies but strategic components of national development . <p> Nigeria should draw an important lesson from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ disasters occur . It must be built steadily through knowledge , research and institutional capacity . <p> The country already possesses part of that scientific infrastructure . The National Water Resources Institute ( NWRI ) serves as the Federal Ministry of Water Resources and Sanitation 's principal institution for research , professional training and technical support in water resources management . It also hosts UNESCO 's Regional Centre for Integrated River Basin Management for West Africa under UNESCO 's Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme , reflecting international recognition of Nigeria 's potential contribution to regional water governance . <p> The Institute 's significance , however , lies not merely in its international affiliations but in the broader role institutions of its kind play within national development . <p> As climate change intensifies , these functions become even more important . <p> Nigeria 's agriculture , energy , industry , urban water supply and public health all depend on reliable water resources , making effective water management essential for economic stability and climate resilience . <p> Investing in water science is therefore not simply an environmental expenditure . It is an investment in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ health . <p> International evidence strongly supports this conclusion . UNESCO has consistently argued that strengthening hydrological science and scientific capacity is indispensable for climate adaptation , while the World Meteorological Organisation continues to emphasise that investments in hydrological observation networks and multi-hazard early-warning systems save lives and reduce long-term economic losses . Every naira invested in preparedness is invariably less expensive than rebuilding roads , bridges , schools and homes after preventable disasters . <p> Unfortunately , Nigeria has historically devoted greater political attention to disaster response than to disaster prevention . <p> Budgets for emergency interventions often receive greater visibility than investments in research institutions , scientific equipment , monitoring networks and professional training . This imbalance reflects a governance culture that rewards immediate political responses to crises while underestimating the long-term value of scientific knowledge . <p> Changing this mindset is essential . <p> Scientific institutions should be central to Nigeria 's climate strategy . Their research must inform policy , strengthen collaboration across government and academia , and be communicated in practical ways that enable policymakers , farmers and communities to make informed decisions . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ journals or institutional reports . <p> Climate change will increasingly test Nigeria 's resilience . The choice is simple : continue reacting after disasters or invest in the scientific capacity needed to anticipate , reduce and manage climate risks . <p> That choice will shape the country 's future . <p> Nigeria can not build climate resilience through emergency relief alone . It requires sustained investment in water science , in strengthening institutions like the National Water Resources Institute alongside research centres and hydrological agencies across the country that generate evidence for sound policymaking . As climate change intensifies , strengthening scientific capacity is a strategic investment in national resilience . Nigeria can either continue paying the cost of recurring disasters or invest in the science that helps prevent them .

@@139176406 <h> Beyond Employment : Why Nigeria Must Build Civic Capability <p> Volunteerism , innovation and civic capability may be Nigeria 's most overlooked workforce development strategy . <p> Every year , hundreds of thousands of young Nigerians graduate with ambition , qualifications and hope . Yet for many , the transition from education to meaningful work remains uncertain -- not simply because jobs are scarce , but because the capabilities increasingly demanded by today 's economy are rarely developed through formal education alone . <p> In an era marked by artificial intelligence , climate change and shifting labour markets , the question is no longer simply whether young people will find jobs , it is whether they are being equipped with the consciousness to create value in a rapidly changing world . <p> This global shift demands a fundamental rethink of how societies prepare young people for work . The World Economic Forum 's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies analytical thinking , resilience , creativity , leadership , technological literacy and lifelong learning among the fastest-growing workforce capabilities . These are not merely technical competencies ; they are deeply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ meaningfully across sectors . <p> Yet a growing disconnect persists between education and employment . According to the International Labour Organization , one in five young people globally are not in employment , education or training ( NEET ) , underscoring that the challenge extends beyond job creation to the effectiveness of pathways that prepare young people for meaningful work . <p> For Africa , this challenge carries both urgency and opportunity . <p> Advertisement <p> Home to the world 's youngest and fastest-growing population , Africa is projected to account for an increasing share of the global workforce over the coming decades . This demographic dividend has the potential to drive innovation , entrepreneurship and sustainable economic growth . However , it is not population size that determines prosperity , it is the systems that develop people 's capabilities . <p> Across the continent , employers consistently report shortages in practical skills such as problem-solving , communication , collaboration and adaptability . While investments in education have expanded access to learning , many graduates continue to struggle with the transition from classrooms to workplaces . Too often , academic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ real-world settings . <p> This is particularly evident in Nigeria as one of the youngest countries in the world , with roughly two-thirds of its population under the age of 25 . Nigeria possesses one of the largest youth populations globally . Every year , hundreds of thousands of graduates enter an increasingly competitive labour market where traditional employment opportunities can not keep pace with demand . While unemployment and underemployment remain pressing concerns , they are symptoms of a broader challenge : the need to strengthen the capabilities that enable young people to create opportunities , lead change and respond to evolving economic realities . <p> Preparing young people for the future of work therefore requires expanding our understanding of workforce development . It is not enough to focus solely on formal employment . We must also invest in the experiences that cultivate leadership , innovation , civic responsibility and practical problem-solving . <p> Nigeria 's future competitiveness will depend not only on the jobs it creates but on the capabilities it cultivates . It places young people in environments where they learn to manage projects , work with diverse stakeholders , communicate effectively , adapt to complex challenges and develop solutions rooted in community realities . These are precisely the capabilities increasingly sought by employers , entrepreneurs and global institutions alike . <p> This broader understanding of volunteerism has gained global recognition . Countries such as Germany and Switzerland have long recognised the value of experiential learning through dual education systems that combine classroom instruction with practical workplace experience . While their models may differ , they share a common principle : meaningful learning happens through participation , shared responsibility and real-world application . <p> Nigeria already possesses an important foundation in this regard through the National Youth Service Corps ( NYSC ) . <p> Advertisement <p> For over five decades , NYSC has mobilised graduates to serve communities across the country . @@139188403 <p> The true measure of governance is rarely found in speeches . It is found in the water that reaches a tap , the flood that does not come , the tree that shades a street and provide an improved air quality , the clean environment devoid of waste . By that standard , Kano State has spent the past three years writing a quieter , sturdier kind of political record , one built less on rhetoric than on boreholes drilled , treatment plants restored , drains dug and seedlings planted . <p> Under Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf , the Kano State Ministry of Water Resources , Environment and Climate Change has pursued what may be the most ambitious environmental and water-sector transformation programme attempted by any state in northern Nigeria . It has not always made headlines . Infrastructure : roads , bridges , schools , tends to command public attention in a way that borehole construction and rehabilitation , sweeping the roads and streets , drainages and canals construction and distilling and tree nurseries do not . But the investments made here may prove just as consequential to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ healthy , and how the state weathers the decades ahead . <p> Climate change is no longer an abstraction for policymakers in the Sahel 's shadow . Erratic rainfall , flash flooding , encroaching desertification and rising pressure on water resources are now lived realities across Nigeria 's north . Governments face a choice : manage these crises as they arrive , or build the institutions to anticipate them . Kano has opted for the latter , and has the paperwork to prove it . The state has developed and adopted a Climate Change Policy , validated a Climate Change Implementation Plan and a Climate Finance Reform Action Plan running through 2028 , while a Climate Change Bill alongside a companion regulation on environmental pollution and waste , translated into Hausa for wider public reach is now before stakeholders . Institutional reform of this kind rarely draws applause , but it is what allows a state to attract serious climate financing rather than simply react to the next disaster . <p> It is telling , too , that the Governor chose to merge the portfolios of Water Resources , Environment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , environmental protection and climate resilience are not three separate problems ; they are one interconnected challenge , and Kano 's institutional structure now reflects that . <h> RELATED NEWS <p> Nowhere is the case for implementation over rhetoric clearer than in water . After years of ageing infrastructure and recurring shortages , the administration has moved on two fronts at once : immediate relief and long-term rebuilding . <p> The immediate relief has come through the approval of 166 solar-powered boreholes targeted at communities facing acute shortages , expected to yield more than 4.15 million litres of potable water daily and reach an estimated 830,000 residents , powered by renewable energy rather than the diesel generators that typically strain such schemes over time this is in addition to over 1000 hand pump boreholes . <p> The long-term rebuilding is larger in scale and consequence : multibillion naira is committed to the rehabilitation and upgrading of the Tamburawa and Challawa Water Treatment Plants , along with the restoration of raw water pumping stations and the Goron Dutse Reservoirs . Once complete , this work is expected to materially expand water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ day and restore reliable pipe-borne supply across Kano metropolis and its surrounding communities , the kind of unglamorous , capital-intensive project whose value tends to be felt years after the ribbon-cutting , not at it . <p> Flood control tells a similar story of scale meeting intent . Community-based drainage clearance has reached 88 metropolitan wards . Major channels : Jakara , Kwarin Gogau , Babban Gwari among many have undergone large-scale desilting , backed by new drainage construction targeting the city 's worst flood-prone corridors . No city sitting in Kano 's climate can eliminate flooding outright ; what can be achieved , and what appears to be happening , is a measurable reduction in its frequency and severity , along with erosion-control work now extending to priority gully sites state-wide . <p> The environmental restoration effort runs on a similar logic of scale . Government nurseries have raised roughly 10 million tree seedlings , more than five million of which have already gone into the ground across the state , complemented by greening along major metropolitan road corridors and public-space planting in schools , markets and religious centres @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 8,100 metric tonnes evacuated , the Dorayi compost plant recommissioned to convert organic waste into fertiliser , and a waste-to-wealth framework designed to draw private capital into what has traditionally been treated as a purely public burden . None of this is glamorous work . It is , however , the work that determines whether a growing city stays liveable . <p> The Ministry 's own accounting suggests it understands that environmental and water stewardship can not be legislated from above alone . Community engagement now spans more than 500 groups and institutions ; an NYSC Climate Change Community Development Service has been established to draw young corps members into the work ; and a digital public-awareness campaign has taken the ministry 's social media following from zero to over 30,000 , generating more than ten million engagements along the way . Whatever one makes of the raw numbers , the underlying strategy , treating residents as participants in environmental and water governance rather than its passive beneficiaries , is the right one , and increasingly rare in African subnational governance . <p> The clearest external validation of this record @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ national climate governance rankings , a jump that reflects institutional credibility as much as any single project , and one likely to matter more over time as it opens doors to climate finance and technical partnerships that lower-ranked states will struggle to access . <p> the trajectory is the story here , and it is an encouraging one . What the Kano State Ministry of Water Resources , Environment and Climate Change has demonstrated over three years is that water security and environmental governance , done seriously , are not soft add-ons to development , they are public health policy , economic policy and long-term security policy in one . As states across Nigeria confront the same climate and water pressures with far less institutional groundwork , Kano 's approach merged mandates , integrated policy , sustained investment , and governance treated as a shared civic project , offers a template worth examining , whatever one 's politics . <p> Governments are usually remembered for what they build . The more durable legacy , often , is what they were disciplined enough to protect . <p> Editor 's note : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Water Resources , Environment and Climate Change 's three-year project record ( 2023 -- 2026 ) .

@@139326579 <h> Strategic imperative of global business summits on Africa , by Ehi Braimah <p> Africa has emerged as one of the most strategic frontiers for global investment , trade , innovation , and economic transformation . With a population projected to exceed 2.5 billion by 2050 , abundant natural resources , a rapidly expanding middle class , and the world 's youngest workforce , the continent is increasingly attracting the attention of governments , multinational corporations , investors , development institutions , and entrepreneurs . Against this backdrop , global business summits hosted in Africa and across the world in Africa , have become vital platforms for dialogue , partnership-building , and economic cooperation . <p> From investment forums and trade expos to leadership conferences and innovation summits , these gatherings bring together policymakers , business executives , financiers , academics , and development experts to discuss opportunities and challenges shaping Africa 's future . Beyond networking events , they have become powerful instruments for driving economic growth , fostering regional integration , and positioning Africa as a key player in the global economy . <p> The summits on Africa @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ known as Africa Future Forward Summit , held in Nairobi , Kenya from May 11 to 12 for the first time in an Anglophone country . It was followed by Biashara Afrika in Lome , Togo , which held from May 18 to 22 , while the London-Africa Business Summit convened by Sadiq Khan , the Mayor of London , held on June 4 . The London Summit attracted diaspora professionals , international investors , and policymakers to discuss the harmonisation of capital markets , tech investments and economic growth in Africa . <p> On July 30 , the Global Africa Summit will hold at the Toronto Metropolitan University , Toronto , Canada . The summit will focus on translating Canada 's Africa Strategy into tangible trade , fintech , infrastructure , and green energy by connecting institutional investors with emerging African markets . <p> Other major and annual recurring events include the US-Africa Business Summit holding in Mauritius from July 26 to 29 , co-hosted by the Corporate Council on Africa and the Government of Mauritius ; the Opportunities in Africa Summit in New York City where investors and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ high-growth markets like Rwanda , Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire . <p> There 's also the US-Africa Leaders ' Summit in Washington DC , USA ; the Africa CEO Forum , the Climate Change Global Business Summit on Africa which holds in Nairobi , Kenya ; the Financial Times ( FT ) Africa Summit that will hold from October 21 to 22 , at The Landmark , London ; the Transform Africa Summit , the continent 's premier annual forum on technology , innovation and digital transformation organised by Smart Africa Alliance , and others . <p> These summits provide a unique platform for governments to showcase investment opportunities and policy reforms aimed at attracting FDI . Investors , in turn , gain valuable insights into emerging markets , regulatory environments , and sector-specific opportunities . For local businesses , the events offer exposure to international markets , potential partners , and financing sources . <p> The role of AfCFTA <p> The African Continental Free Trade Area ( AfCFTA ) should be the economic anchor of every Africa-focused global business summit . Whether in Abuja , Lagos , Nairobi , Kigali @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Washington DC , Dubai , Moscow , or Beijing , AfCFTA must be presented not merely as a trade agreement but as Africa 's blueprint for industrialisation , regional value chains and a single market of over 1.4 billion people . <p> A united AfCFTA agenda will strengthen Africa 's bargaining power , reduce trade barriers , create jobs and position the continent as a competitive global investment destination . Africa 's economic transformation depends on making AfCFTA the centrepiece of every international business engagement . <p> Benefits <p> One of the most significant benefits of global business summits is their ability to attract investment . Many investment deals , public-private partnerships , and development projects originate from conversations initiated during these events . By bringing together key decision-makers in one location , summits reduce barriers to engagement and facilitate quicker decision-making . <p> Business summits also stimulate tourism and local economic activity . Hotels , transportation services , restaurants , event management firms , and other service providers benefit from the influx of delegates . Host cities often gain international visibility , improving their reputation as business and investment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ building . Young entrepreneurs , startups , and small and medium-sized enterprises ( SMEs ) gain opportunities to learn from industry leaders , access mentorship , and connect with investors . This helps nurture the next generation of African business leaders and innovators . <p> On a broader scale , global business summits support economic diplomacy . Governments use these platforms to strengthen bilateral and multilateral relationships , negotiate trade agreements , and promote regional cooperation . Such engagements can lead to long-term economic partnerships that benefit multiple countries . <p> Africa 's strategic importance in the global economy <p> The increasing number of global business summits on Africa reflects the continent 's growing strategic importance . Africa possesses approximately 30 percent of the world 's mineral reserves , including critical minerals such as cobalt , lithium , manganese , and rare earth elements that are essential for electric vehicles , renewable energy technologies , and advanced manufacturing . <p> In addition , Africa 's agricultural potential remains largely untapped . The continent holds vast areas of arable land capable of contributing significantly to global food security . Its expanding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the most promising growth markets in the world . <p> The continent 's digital revolution further enhances its attractiveness . Mobile technology , fintech innovation , e-commerce , and digital payment systems have transformed business operations across many African countries such as Nigeria and Kenya . Investors increasingly view Africa not only as a source of raw materials but also as a market for innovation and technological advancement . <p> The new scramble for Africa <p> The growing international interest in Africa has led many analysts to describe current geopolitical and economic competition as a " New Scramble for Africa . " Unlike the colonial-era scramble of the late nineteenth century , today 's competition is driven primarily by economic , technological , and strategic interests rather than direct territorial control . <p> Major global powers , including the United States , China , the European Union , India , Turkey , Russia , and Gulf states , are actively expanding their engagement across Africa . They compete for access to natural resources , infrastructure projects , trade opportunities , energy partnerships , digital markets , and geopolitical influence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trading partners and infrastructure financiers , investing heavily in roads , railways , ports , and industrial parks . Western nations have responded by increasing investment initiatives focused on sustainable development , clean energy , digital infrastructure , and private sector growth . Meanwhile , emerging powers are seeking to deepen commercial and diplomatic ties through trade agreements , investment missions , and development partnerships . <p> Global business summits often serve as arenas where these competing interests intersect . International corporations and governments use such forums to announce investment commitments , launch strategic partnerships , and strengthen economic relationships with African nations . <p> While increased global attention creates opportunities for growth and development , it also presents challenges . African countries must ensure that investments contribute to sustainable development , local job creation , technology transfer , and industrialisation . Effective governance , transparency , and strategic negotiation are essential to ensuring that Africa derives maximum benefit from foreign engagement . <p> Africa 's future <p> As Africa 's economic influence continues to grow , global business summits will play an increasingly important role in shaping the continent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , innovation exchange , policy dialogue , and international cooperation . They also help position African countries as active participants in global economic decision-making rather than passive recipients of external interests . <p> The challenge and opportunity for Africa lie in leveraging these platforms to advance its own development priorities . By fostering strategic partnerships , promoting intra-African trade , supporting entrepreneurship , and ensuring inclusive growth , business summits can become powerful catalysts for transformation . <p> In the context of the new scramble for Africa , the continent is no longer merely a destination for external interests . Increasingly , it is becoming a dynamic actor with the capacity to shape global markets , influence international investment flows , and define its own development trajectory . <p> Global business summits on Africa provide one of the most visible and effective mechanisms through which this transformation can be realised . <p> . @@139386511 <p> For years , insecurity has cast a long shadow over governance in Nigeria , particularly across the northern states .
